articles.title: EU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter China
articles.summary:
Authorities and public bodies to be urged to buy goods and services from Europe, but without binding quotas

European authorities will be encouraged to buy more domestic goods and services…

blocks.text: European authorities will be encouraged to buy more domestic goods and services when they spend public money under the EU latest effort to counter China’s economic might.
In a further “Buy European” plan, the European Commission published proposals on Wednesday for a sweeping overhaul of EU public procurement rules.

National authorities and public bodies, such as schools and hospitals, will be encouraged to buy goods and services made in Europe but, unlike earlier plans to promote domestically manufactured clean tech, there will be no binding “made in Europe” quotas.

Brussels officials are concerned that many public agencies think existing EU rules oblige them to choose the cheapest bid when spending public money, which can lead to the contract going to a non-European firm.

The European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, Stéphane Séjourné, told reporters the regulation would give public sector buyers greater legal certainty and clarity about purchasing goods and services made in Europe.

“Purchasers can have a more preferential approach to European bids [and] restrict or reject bids from countries which do not have a public procurement agreement or do not play by binding rules in terms of public procurement internationally,” he said.

Séjourné hopes the proposals will encourage more democratic scrutiny over the spending of public money by local authorities. “It won’t be the European Commission’s fault if purchasers were to prefer Chinese buses to European buses because … in the [draft regulation] there is every possibility to give preference to European buses.”

blocks.caption: Stéphane Séjourné, who it the European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, is a close ally of Emmanuel Macron. Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPA

blocks.text: Brussels is concerned about inroads Beijing is making into European markets for transport and infrastructure, especially Chinese firms benefitting from state subsidies that make them cheaper than European alternatives.

In April, the commission blocked a Chinese rolling-stock company from joining a consortium to build a new line on the Lisbon metro after an investigation found the firm had benefited from state subsidies that gave it an “unfair competitive edge”.

Last year, Brussels opened an investigation into Chinese security company Nuctech, which has supplied European airports and ports with security scanners. EU officials suspect the company was helped by subsidies and tax breaks that gave it an unfair advantage in the European market, although the investigation has not reached final conclusions.

Séjourné – a close ally of France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, who has long championed European preference – said spending public money on goods made in Europe should become “part of public discourse and accountability”.
He added: “It should be very clear that it’s not because of European Union rules that a foreign product was preferred over a European one, but because it was a political choice that was made.”

The draft regulation, which also aims to radically simplify rules by merging three laws into one, must be agreed by the European parliament and the EU ministers before it enters into force. It is likely to be altered during the legislative process.

Séjourné is also spearheading a push for made-in-Europe rules to apply to the public purchase of renewable energy products and electric cars under the the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, which also is likely to be changed by MEPs and ministers, marks a departure for Brussels, long a bastion of open markets.

The plans have alarmed the British government, but EU officials said the latest draft rules on procurement would not disadvantage UK firms because existing agreements ensured both sides played by the same rules.
after newsletter promotion
Séjourne said the EU had agreements with the UK whereby reciprocal market access was respected. “There should not be any difficulties for the UK,” he added.
Non-EU countries that have agreements with the bloc on public procurement are not expected to face barriers.
An online tool will allow public purchasers to see which countries are covered by the EU’s web of free-trade agreements and other international deals that cover procurement.

Membership of the World Trade Organization’s agreement on government procurement (GPA), which promotes fair competition in markets to supply state bodies, will be an important indicator. The GPA has 22 members including the EU (counted as one), the UK, the US, Canada and Japan. Mainland China is not party to the agreement.

Public procurement is estimated by EU officials to amount to 15% of the bloc’s gross domestic product, about €2.6tn (£2.2tn) a year, and is seen in Brussels as an underused lever already deployed by Washington and Beijing to support their respective domestic companies.
The new rules will oblige public buyers in the EU to put more emphasis on quality and metrics such as environmental sustainability and local supply chains, rather than opting for the cheapest bid.
Under the proposals public agencies will be obliged to give a minimum 30% weighting to quality when they draw up conditions to award a contract, or explain why they chose to disregard this indicator.
Labour-intensive contracts will have a minimum 50% weighting for quality, so purchasers must ensure decent jobs when awarding the contract, not simply the cheapest price.

articles.title: N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog
articles.summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency's says the facility is cause for "serious concern".

blocks.text: North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility, the head of the world's nuclear watchdog said this week, calling it a cause for "serious concern".
The new building is part of the main Yongbyon nuclear complex, and reportedly capable of housing up to 28 centrifuge cascades used to enrich uranium.
In a report published late last month, the International Atomic Energy Agency said Pyongyang has also begun operating an expanded annex at another enrichment site.

These findings point to a steady expansion of the North's sancitoned nuclear infrastructure. The agency, which has no inspectors in North Korea since it was expelled in 2009, relies on satellite imagery for assessments.

"The continuation and further development of the DPRK's nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," IAEA director Rafael Grossi said in a statement earlier this week.
The IAEA first referred to the existence of the building in June, although Grossi had mentioned the possibility earlier in the year.
In June, the agency said that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a "newly inaugurated nuclear materials production factory" on 3 June, which it identified as the Yongbyon enrichment facility.
Kim had praised the country's "greatly expanded production capacity", adding that this would "offer the possibility of carrying out larger plans", according to the agency's report.
Despite running one the poorest countries in the world, Kim spends millions each year developing a secretive nuclear arsenal. A 2022 report by a non-proliferation think-tank put this figure at $640m.

"What makes North Korea's nuclear programme so concerning is that many of its facilities are unknown, concealed, and thus difficult to target," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford told the BBC.

"Beyond Yongbyon, we know that other facilities exist: Kangson, for instance. The embeddedness of North Korea's nuclear doctrine within its foreign and domestic policy means that we should expect there to be more concealed production sites."

The agency also said there were indications that operations had started at another enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, in January this year. An annex had first been constructed in Kangson in 2024, it said.
It had said in April that North Korea appeared to be stepping up its ability to make nuclear bombs, saying they were monitoring the apparent expansion of Yongbyon.

The North's nuclear programme has accelerated under Kim, who has overseen a record number of missile tests. The country has fired has numerous intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) since it began testing its long-range system in 2017.
The country has conducted six nuclear weapons tests so far, the last of which was in September 2017.

articles.title: UK airport disruption: what are your rights if you have been affected?
articles.summary: Air traffic control issue affecting UK airports on Tuesday has been resolved, but disruption continues into Wednesday

blocks.text: Airports across the UK including Manchester, Birmingham and all those in London were hit by problems at air traffic control on Tuesday, which continued into Wednesday.

The technical issue was announced shortly before 2pm and was resolved about three hours later. By that time, hundreds of flights had been cancelled, with knock-on disruption across Britain and at destination airports abroad.
The total number of cancellations passed 1,900 on Wednesday after hundreds more flights were axed. Here we explain what you can expect if you have been affected.
Is your flight delayed or cancelled?

The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) website explains how long the delay has to be before you are entitled to care and assistance from your airline while you wait. The timeframe differs by flight distance. This assistance should cover food and drink and the ability to make phone calls or send emails, plus accommodation and the necessary transfers if the flight is delayed until the next day.

Many airlines will provide vouchers for you to buy food and drink, and overnight accommodation will typically take the form of a nearby hotel (unless you live nearby, in which case your airline may reimburse your costs for getting to and from home).
Sometimes airline staff are unable to arrange care and assistance for all passengers, in which case you can sort yourself out and claim the cost back later.

But don’t splash the cash – and keep receipts. The CAA says airlines may have guidelines on this, adding: “Airlines are unlikely to consider alcoholic drinks, luxury hotels or luxury meals to be reasonable.”

If your flight has been cancelled and is covered by UK law – that means one departing from an airport in the UK on any airline, or arriving at an airport in the UK on an EU or UK airline, or arriving at an airport in the EU on a UK airline – your airline must offer you the choice of another flight or a refund.
If you select an alternative flight, it is up to you whether you fly as soon as possible or at a later date.
If the delay is more than five hours you can choose not to travel and receive a refund.
I am due to fly imminently – should I still go to the airport?
If you are due to travel on Wednesday check the latest advice from your airport or tour operator, or airline apps and airport social media feeds, for the most up-to-date information.

The air traffic control service provider Nats had advised that it would “take some time” to rectify the problem but at about 5pm on Tuesday it posted on social media that it had “implemented a fix ​and our flight system ⁠is starting to recover”. The knock on impact on flight schedules could take some time to be resolved.
Will I be entitled to compensation from the airline?

If your flight was cancelled or delayed as a result of Tuesday’s issue, you are unlikely to be owed compensation by the airline. This is because the technical issue affecting flights will be considered an extraordinary circumstance and out of the airline’s control.
Causes of disruption classed as outside an airline’s control also include severe weather and security alerts.

Anna-Marie Duthie, a travel insurance expert at the financial ratings company Defaqto, says: “Travel insurance may cover you if you cannot claim costs back from the airline, operator, or credit card but that will all depend on whether your policy includes cover for delay, travel disruption, missed connection or abandonment.”

articles.title: Conflicting court rulings on Missouri map threaten November’s election | First Thing
articles.summary:
The state can’t use new congressional districts under one court order – or its old ones under another. Plus, the architects in Europe turning urban spaces into areas of climate respite

Good…

blocks.text: Good morning. Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty less than two months before the November midterms that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress.

Conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh denied the emergency request from Missouri officials to use a congressional map in November that was redrawn with Donald Trump’s support to give Republicans an edge in the midterms, but a ruling by a federal judge in Missouri temporarily prevented the state from using its old congressional maps.

items: Why is there legal action over the maps? The Missouri supreme court has previously ruled that the new map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, meaning it cannot be used in time for the November election. The president and Republicans had fumed over the decision, with Trump calling it “horrible, ridiculous, and unconstitutional”.

What are the significant changes to the map intended to favor Republicans? The revised map targeted the fifth congressional district, held by longtime Democratic representative Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas.

blocks.text: Israel to close British consulate in Jerusalem after UK imposes sanctions on West Bank settlements

blocks.caption: Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, speaks at the House of Commons in London. Photograph: House Of Commons/Reuters

blocks.text: The UK government has entered a diplomatic row with Israel after it announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements. In the country’s starkest condemnation since the founding of the Israeli state, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband – whose mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – said settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, claimed the ruling UK Labour party Miliband belongs to was gripped by “Jew hatred”.

items: What has the British prime minister said? Writing in the Guardian, Andy Burnham said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, and that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”. “The measures we are taking,” he said, “are about targeting illegal settlements and increasing the pressure on the Israeli government to change course. We are not imposing sanctions on Israel as a whole.”

How has Israel reacted? Israel has ordered the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem among retaliatory measures including entry bans on several UK lawmakers. The Israeli government added that longstanding British involvement in the training of Palestinian security forces on the West Bank would be terminated. Britain will also be excluded from the US-led Gaza coordination mission.

items: What have been the other developments in the region? articles.title: Syria: How the 'house of sisters' threat split society
articles.summary: Rumor has it that the 'house of sisters' is where kidnapped women from other Syrian sects are forced to convert to Islam. Nobody knows if it really exists, but it's being used to create communal…

image.caption: Protest about abducted Syrian women: Another example of the kinds of rumors circulating is that women from minority communities are being sold as sex slaves Image: Elisa Gestri/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A knock on the door, a muted threat and then they made the decision to leave the country, says Layla, a math teacher and mother-of-three in her 40s.

Until recently, Layla — who didn't want DW to use her full name for security reasons — was living in Damascus, Syria's capital. She and her family are Alawites, the same religious sect as former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad, who are often targeted because they're seen as Assad's allies.

"But we never supported him, his father killed members of my family. We hated him actually," she told DW. Still, she describes feeling fearful when rebel groups entered Damascus in 2024 for the first time after the fall of the Assad regime, calling them "extremists."
At first, she and her husband decided to stay in Syria. But then a stranger came to the door.
"He told me 'we know your daughter plays piano and has dance lessons. You should stop that. If you don't, maybe we will take her to the house of the sisters," Layla recounts.

In conservative Islamic circles, women playing music and dancing for an audience is frowned upon. And Layla had heard about the so-called "house of the sisters" — she had read online it was a place where Syrian women from other sects were forced to convert to Islam. A few days later, the family decided to leave the country. They are now in Lebanon.
"I just don't want my children to grow up that way," Layla explains.
What is the 'house of sisters'?

Headlines about the "house of sisters" first really made waves in Syria in May after an Alawite university student Batoul Alloush, 21, was reported missing by her family, possibly kidnapped, only to turn up later wearing religious clothing and saying she left her family in order to convert to Islam.
There were already other stories of missing women, including from the Alawite minority.

Reham Suleiman, a psychologist who works for the United Nations and with the Alawite community, told DW she has firsthand knowledge of several cases of kidnapping. "And it’s not just one incident or coincidence," she says. It is clear some of women were kidnapped for ransom money, revenge or forced marriage.

But other cases were apparently resolved when, for example, the women said they had been visiting friends, wanted to escape their families or had run away to a lover. Alloush herself said she wished to convert to Islam and leave her family. Her parents insist she's been drugged or coerced.
Organizations like Amnesty International and the UN's Commission of Inquiry on Syria say the cases — which number between 40 and 60 ­­— have not been fully investigated.
A political football

Syrian authorities did look into the "house of sisters." A spokesperson for Syria's Minister of Social Affairs, Hind Kabawat, told DW that the ministry has not licensed any facility with that name and that any unlicensed centers of this nature would be shut down.
Syrian fact-checking organizations like Verify-Sy found that pictures of the supposed "house of sisters" building were created with AI.

"A constant stream of unverified claims circulates on a daily basis concerning alleged kidnappings and killings, arrests and cases of torture in detention facilities," a spokesperson from Verify-Sy told DW.
"Verifying many of these is challenging when evidence available through open sources is scarce, contradictory or otherwise insufficient."

So whether the "house of sisters" exists in some form is unclear. But real or not, some groups appear to have instrumentalized it for their own agenda anyway, independent media outlet Shaam News Network, or SNN, wrote recently.

"Despite the absence of any physical evidence … social media platforms and pages began circulating 'the house' as an established fact," SNN wrote. "And it gradually became the focus of broader narratives about the 'organized kidnapping' of Alawite women."
International influencers

A private organization called the Syrian Investigation Mechanism, or SIM, founded in May 2026, links the "house of sisters" to a Muslim organization that proselytizes to gain new converts. SIM claimed the missing women were coerced into converting and held in "the house."

In an interview on YouTube, SIM director Yasser Shalati, who is based in Brandenburg, Germany, claims this is evidence of "demographic engineering." SIM did not reply to DW's requests for further comment.

blocks.caption: Christian neighborhood in Damascus: There have been reports of more attempts to convert others to Islam since the fall of the Assad regime, which treated proselytizing as a threat to national security Image: Mohammad Bashir Aldaher/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: A Berlin-based organization, the Union of Syrian Alawites in Europe, or USAE, has also repeatedly posted about the "house of sisters."

On his personal Facebook page, Muaiad Ibrahim, who is listed as USAE's deputy director in official court documents, regularly criticizes the new Syrian government and recently expressed support for Syria's highest religious scholar under the Assad regime, Ahmed Hassoun. In late August, Hassoun was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of inciting civil war and complicity in intentional killing.

Other recently founded overseas organizations — including some that claim they have a network of millions of human rights advocates but link to incomplete websites — have also repeatedly disseminated stories about the "house of sisters."
Arab investigative journalism outfit DARAJ notes some of these organizations have been criticized for their apparent support of the Assad regime.
The damage done?

"This kind of information ebbs and flows, but it does have a real impact and its quite powerful," says Gregory Waters, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, who's traveled extensively in Syria and monitors events on his site, Syria Revisited.

"It has the political intent to isolate Alawites, to make them fearful and keep them from engaging with the government, with [Syrian] Sunnis, and maybe to some extent, pull them towards insurgent [anti-government] networks."
Online propaganda feeds on real events within minority communities, adding to their existing fears, he says.

Verify Sy conducts a monthly audit of online disinformation, and researchers there say incitement is the second most common objective. Waters says Syrian authorities have been trying to rein in local influencers who spread disinformation, although obviously they can't impact those based overseas.

blocks.caption: Syrians are still finding mass graves after 14 years of a civil war that has resulted in polarized opinions among localsImage: Ugur Yildirim/DIA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Like anywhere else in the world, you'll get a wide spectrum of opinions within every Syrian community, Waters notes. "There are there those who will insist that there's a program of ethnic cleansing, and there are others who say life is fine, we are fully integrated into the state."
Although it depends which part of the country you're looking at, he doesn't think relations between different communities are getting worse.

"In Syria, everything is unique to its local environment," Waters explains. "So in some places, we could say that walls between communities have hardened over the past two years and little progress has been made in reducing that. But even so, the walls are not getting higher."
Stabilization first

"Right now, generally speaking, the government in Damascus is busy establishing institutions, taking control of the security situation and trying to stabilize the country," argues Naseef Naeem, research director at the Berlin-based Candid Foundation, which consults on Syrian affairs. But sooner or later, Syria is going to need more of a national dialogue between different community groups, he says.
In the meantime, both he and Waters believe the Syrian economy, devastated after years of war, could hold the key to better relations.

blocks.caption: Every summer, Latakia's beaches in western Syria are a popular destination for thousands of Syrian holidaymakers Image: Elisa Gestri/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "As soon as the economic recovery really gets underway, many of these phenomena will gradually disappear," Naeem told DW.
For example, Waters says, over summer, a lot of domestic tourists, many of them Sunni, made their way to the Syrian coast, an area where many Alawites live.

"There was a massive tourism boom," Waters explains. "Everybody's interacting and I've heard from friends there that there wasn't harassment, no violence. The government and security authorities really emphasized supporting the tourism industry in coastal areas this year and it's had a really positive impact."
Those kinds of inter-community contacts in real life "help reduce the impact of disinformation campaigns and the level of fear," he concludes.

articles.title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win
articles.summary: Germany's chancellor clashes with AfD leader Alice Weidel, saying her migration policy amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images/Reuters
Merz and Weidel faced off for the first time since Sunday's AfD election victory
ByPaul Kirby
Europe digital editor

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.
Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.
Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.

It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.

The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.

Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".
While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it make a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.
Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."

Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.

blocks.caption: Map of eastern Germany highlighting the state of Saxony-Anhalt in white. Key locations marked include Magdeburg (the state capital), Querfurt and Leipzig within or near the highlighted area, and Berlin to the northeast. Poland is shown to the east and the Czech Republic to the south. An inset map…

blocks.text: As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.
Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.

"You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.
The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.

Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.

articles.title: SWS: 48% of Filipinos expect quality of life to improve in next 12 months
articles.summary: Forty-eight percent of Filipinos aged 18 and above believe their quality of life will improve in the next 12 months, according to the latest survey by the Social Weather Stations (SWS).

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 7:23pm
Forty-eight percent of Filipinos aged 18 and above believe their quality of life will improve in the next 12 months, according to the latest survey by the Social Weather Stations (SWS).
The poll classified the 48% of respondents who expected improvements in their quality of life as “optimists.”
Meanwhile, 31% said their quality of life would remain the same, while 8% or the “pessimists” expected it to worsen.
The remaining 12% did not give an answer.

These figures resulted in a net personal optimism score of +40, computed by subtracting the percentage of pessimists from the percentage of optimists. SWS classified the score as “excellent,” according to SWS.
The June 2026 score was 17 points higher than the “high” +23 recorded in March, the survey firm said.
“The 17-point increase in the national Net Personal Optimism score between March and June 2026 was due to gains in all areas,” SWS said.
Net Personal Optimism rose from “high” to “excellent” in Balance Luzon, increasing by 27 points from +22 to +49.
The score also rose from “high” to “very high” in Metro Manila, up by 8 points from +28 to +36; in the Visayas, up by 6 points from +27 to +33; and in Mindanao, up by 11 points from +20 to +31.

The non-commissioned survey was conducted from June 20 to 29 and interviewed 1,200 adults face-to-face: 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas and Mindanao, and 600 in Balance Luzon, or Luzon outside Metro Manila.
The sampling error margins are ±3 percentage points for national percentages and ±6 percentage points each for Metro Manila, Balance Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Cesafi’s former No. 1 high school player starts new chapter with UP Cebu
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — Kenneth Fuller spent four years building his name in Cesafi high school basketball. Now, he is starting all over again. The former No. 1 high school player in the Cebu…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — Kenneth Fuller spent four years building his name in Cesafi high school basketball.

Now, he is starting all over again. The former No. 1 high school player in the Cebu Schools Athletic Foundation, Inc. (Cesafi) in Season 25 has entered Season 26 as a rookie with the University of the Philippines (UP) Cebu Fighting Maroons, trading the expectations of high school stardom for the challenges of college basketball.

A year ago, many Cebuano basketball fans expected Fuller to win the MVP award after he dominated almost every major statistical category, based on the Samahang Basketbol ng Pilipinas (SBP) Zone 8’s real-time data.

It did not happen, but Fuller has moved on. His focus now is UP Cebu, which opened its Season 26 campaign with an 0-2 record, including a 26-point collapse against the CIT-U Wildcats after building a big lead.
For Fuller, the rough start is part of the adjustment.
“As a rookie, I put pressure on myself that I wouldn’t just settle for the quality minutes usually given to rookies. I don’t want to underperform in every minute I have on the floor,” Fuller said.
“I’ve already adjusted to the intensity of college basketball, and I can say that I can play competitively alongside older players on the floor.”
The transition, however, has been anything but easy.

“The game was more physical, faster, but through chemistry and practice with the team, I was able to adjust,” Fuller said. “But I admit, I still lack the experience. There are still tendencies that I’m overwhelmed by the intensity of college basketball.”
What Fuller brings with him is the discipline and consistency he developed during four years with the Cebu Eastern College (CEC) Dragons under coaches Rodmark Del Rosario and Mark Tallo.
“It’s definitely the discipline and consistency that my coaches Rodmark and Coach Mark taught me when I was with CEC,” Fuller said.
“Throughout my four years with CEC, I learned and adapted that character and value and carried it to my college basketball career. So, I’m very thankful to CEC.”
With his credentials, many expected Fuller to leave Cebu for a bigger basketball program in Manila. He chose to stay home. For Fuller, the decision was simple.
“My first priority is education, of course. It’s the University of the Philippines. Of course, it’s all about the education they offer. That’s why I played here,” he said.
The basketball system also played a major role. Fuller had seen UP Cebu head coach Rommel Rasmo’s system when he faced his teams in high school.
“I also saw the system of Coach Rommel back when we played against them in high school with Ateneo de Cebu. That’s when I realized that I can fit and shine with his system,” Fuller said.

Now, Fuller is no longer facing Rasmo from across the court. He is learning from him. And while the adjustment continues, the numbers from his final Cesafi high school season show why UP Cebu sees potential in the rookie.
Fuller led all players with 54.3 statistical points, averaging 10.4 points, 8.9 rebounds, 6.8 assists, 3.8 steals and 0.8 blocks per game.
CEC narrowly missed the Final Four through the points quotient tiebreaker.

Fuller missed out on the MVP award. But neither setback defines his next chapter. At UP Cebu, he gets a fresh start, a new system and a chance to prove that his best basketball may still be ahead of him.

articles.title: The problem with replatforming Alfred ‘Krip’ Yuson
articles.summary: Publishing house Exploding Galaxies announces that it will no longer republish and circulate Yuson's novel 'Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café'

blocks.text: Publishing house Exploding Galaxies announces that it will no longer republish and circulate Yuson's novel 'Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café'

items: Filipino author Alfred 'Krip' Yuson has faced multiple allegations of sexual misconduct and a plagiarism case, raising concerns about the ethics of republishing his work, particularly his novel 'Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.'

Despite initial support for the republication from Exploding Galaxies, backlash from the literary community led to a reconsideration of its decision, highlighting the complexities of promoting literature by controversial figures.

The situation has sparked broader discussions within the literary community about the moral implications of supporting works by authors with problematic histories and the responsibilities of publishers in such cases.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino literature and the classics that have come out of it always deserve to be known, and it’s often made possible by efforts like republishing and circulating physical copies to make them accessible to even more readers. But when the author behind one of these books has caused more harm than good, it becomes an entirely different story.
Case in point: Alfred “Krip” Yuson and his 1988 novel Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.

The book was supposed to have been given new life by Exploding Galaxies — with the publishing house even standing by its initial decision to republish the book despite drawing backlash from members of the literary community. Here’s what went down.

Yuson, a Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature Hall of Fame inductee, has been accused of sexual misconduct on several instances by different individuals. His latest published work was the 2022 book The Mountain That Grew.

“Why re-platform a man who’s responsible for the harassment and suicide of women? I do not care how brilliant you think his book is. I DO NOT CARE. And I will NEVER understand,” writer Katrina Stuart Santiago said in a Threads post on August 26.
Santiago further attested that she knows of young female writers who have had their own share of “horrid” experiences at the hands of Yuson.

“I remember when writers were being ‘cancelled’ left and right for everything from minor indiscretions to horrible mistakes to bad decisions, my question then was: when do we talk about the dirty old men of the literary establishment? Because THAT is a list. And it also has a list of victims. Re-platforming one of them by reprinting his book seems like [a] signal, doesn’t it. Of many things, including that people think we forget who these men are. We do not. We cannot. WE SHOULD NOT,” she said in another post on August 27.
Santiago added that literary workshops fuel Yuson’s predatory behavior, given the power dynamics that exist in these spaces between mentors and their mentees.

In response, Exploding Galaxies had initially attempted to discredit Santiago’s commentary, stating that while sexual harassment isn’t something they take lightly, the allegations that have been thrown at Yuson “have not been proven or independently corroborated.”

“We republished Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café for its well-established literary merit, and we stand by our decision to publish the book,” Exploding Galaxies wrote in its first public statement on September 5.

“We also stand firm against dishonest and unfair attempts to discredit this republication, especially as it is coming from a person who has expressed a longstanding personal grudge against the author, and who has, over the years, leveled serious public accusations against others,” it added.

Other figures in the literary community were quick to weigh in on the matter, with award-winning writer Jose “Butch” Dalisay Jr. pondering on the topic of art being created by questionable individuals.

“Does moral or political purity translate to some kind of elevated prose, or more honest and insightful poetry?” he wrote in a Facebook post. “Can someone please put together a library of vetted literature (or otherwise a new Index Librorum Prohibitorium) to spare us the process, and so we can keep to the straight and narrow, and enjoy reading without guilt or shame?”

Dalisay had followed it up with another post apologizing for appearing to trivialize the plight of sexual harassment victims — adding that the phenomenon of enabling a culture of harassment in workshops was something he would take up with the UP Institute of Creative Writing.

“There was a specific context to my remark that sexual misconduct and plagiarism were “low-hanging fruit.” It was not to dismiss them but to suggest that they were, among human evils, among the most visible and most common (which makes them no less painful to those concerned). I was talking about the possible crimes writers and artists have been accused of, which include murder and treason, and other offenses that injure not just one but many,” Dalisay said.

“I apologize to those victims of sexual harassment who may have seen my remarks as dismissive; they were not meant to be. It is a serious problem we are confronting not only in literature but in society at large.”
But sexual harassment isn’t the only serious issue that Yuson has found himself involved in. Writer Jaemark Tordecilla had accused him of plagiarism in 2011.

Tordecilla noticed that Yuson lifted several paragraphs from sportswriter Rey Joble’s piece about former PBA commissioner Rudy Salud. Joble’s story was published under GMA News Online, while Yuson had passed off his own version of it to Rogue Magazine.

Yuson was serving as GMA News Online’s editor-at-large then, and was in charge of copyediting Joble’s draft. He explained that since he had rewritten portions of Joble’s work, he thought he was considered to at least be part-author.

While he apologized for his actions, Yuson had merely attributed them to his old age, being overworked, and the pressure of having to meet deadlines. He still continued to write more after, and had even published several more works, like Islands of Words & Other Poems (2015), The Music Child & The Mahjong Queen (2016), and In the Footsteps of St. Ignatius of Loyola (2017), among others.
On September 7, Exploding Galaxies eventually announced that it would no longer push through with promoting or publishing Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.

“We hear you all. We are sorry for the hurt this has caused our community. We are no longer promoting or releasing this book. As a publisher, we will do better. Thank you for speaking up,” the publisher said.

Exploding Galaxies also promised to “do better” in its mission to put works of Philippine literature back into circulation. But this still begs the question: How can publishers and literary circles do their part in discerning whether or not it is appropriate to promote a piece of work when the individual behind it has caused hurt to many others in the past?
Yuson has yet to comment on the matter himself. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines — Thousands of devotees gathered at the Monastery of the Holy Eucharist (more commonly known as Simala Shrine) in Lindogon, Sibonga, before dawn on Sept. 8 for the annual…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines — Thousands of devotees gathered at the Monastery of the Holy Eucharist (more commonly known as Simala Shrine) in Lindogon, Sibonga, before dawn on Sept. 8 for the annual Mañanita celebrating the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
The gathering featured candle-lighting and prayers as the faithful paid tribute to the Blessed Virgin Mary on her feast day.
Content creator Arlan Obiso Barazona captured the celebration from above at around 2 a.m., showing the Simala Shrine illuminated by candles and surrounded by devotees.
His posts gained online traction, with over 300,000 reactions on Facebook as of this writing, and drew thousands of comments from netizens who extended their greetings to the Blessed Virgin Mary.
The Mañanita, locally known as “Banwag sa Pagkahimugso,” has been held in Simala for years as part of the shrine’s celebration of the Blessed Virgin Mary’s birthday.
Simala is among Cebu’s most recognizable Marian pilgrimage sites, housing the image of Our Lady of Lindogon inside its castle-like monastery.

The image was brought to Cebu in 1997 by the Marian Monks of Eucharistic Adoration (MMEA), six years after a mysterious woman reportedly gave the image to the monks for safekeeping at the height of the 1991 Mt. Pinatubo eruption in Pampanga, as reported by CDN Digital in 2021. ///

articles.title: LIV Golf in financial turmoil: what's next for the sport?
articles.summary: Six months after Saudi Arabia pulled funding from the breakaway organization, LIV Golf have filed for bankruptcy protection. Several of the world's best players signed on to LIV, so where does that…

image.caption: Bryson DeChambeau is owed an estimated $5.7m by LIV GolfImage: Jerod Ringwald/IMAGN Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: What has happened to LIV golf?
The breakaway golf tour, launched with much fanfare, billions of dollars of investment and a string of the world's best players, in 2021. But on Tuesday it filed for bankruptcy protection in the US.

Bankruptcy protection is a way of keeping a company alive while it restructures its debts. In this case, LIV would be moving from being financed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which pulled out in April, to being supported by BC Partners, a British investment firm.
"This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf," said the chief executive, Scott O'Neil.

According to documents related to the filing, LIV Golf has between $500m (€430 million) and $1bn in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors. This includes an estimated $45 million to a group of top players like Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m), Jon Rahm ($7.5m) and Dustin Johnson ($5.7m).

O'Neil added that LIV intends to move towards a "player-first ownership model" but detail is thin and there is currently no schedule in place for 2027. Most of LIV's staff were laid off earlier this year.
What has caused LIV golf to go bankrupt?

The sudden withdrawal of the PIF, which had invested an estimated $5 billion in LIV Golf, is the over-riding reason. At the time, the PIF said that LIV Golf was "no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy."

This was considered evidence of the project's failure to overthrow the established PGA Tour or make much in the way of money or impact. While the huge prize money on offer lured away several big names, many more remained with the PGA Tour.

While Tuesday's legal move may buy LIV time, the withdrawal of Saudi funding was so key to its business model that it gives O'Neil few options. To survive, it seems, they must keep at least some of their big-name players while slimming down dramatically.
Why is Saudi Arabia investing billions in sports?
Is this further evidence of Saudi Arabia pulling out of sport?

It certainly seems that investment in golf is a thing of the past for the oil-rich, Gulf state. There have also been withdrawals of funding for tournaments, clubs or organizations in snooker, women's tennis, rugby and football. Saudi Arabia also backed away from its commitment to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games.

Sport was a key part of Vision 2030, a pet project of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that aimed to diversify the Saudi economy and, in the eyes of many, also help launder its reputation through sport and other cultural assets.

blocks.caption: Saudi Arabia is scaling back many sporting plans, including for World Cup 2034Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: The uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East has meant even the vast wealth of the Saudi ruling class has taken a hit while projects like the resort of Trojena, set to be a key resort in those Winter Games, have been scaled back.

The same is true of Neom, a proposed World Cup venue for 2034. Planned as an entirely new type of city - 500-meter-high, built in a straight line and powered by renewable energy, Neom's construction has been significantly scaled back. The Guardian reported in late 2025 that several proposed World Cup stadium architects have been asked to rethink their plans to cut costs.
What will happen to the LIV golf players now?

That too is unclear. The PGA Tour and LIV Golf have always had a frosty relationship. Any player leaving to join LIV was immediately suspended from the PGA Tour, which runs all golf's major championships.

The 'returning member program', used by US golfer Brooks Koepka earlier this year to return to the PGA, briefly offered a potential pathway. It was designed as a "route back to elite performers who no longer have contractual limitations preventing them from complying with PGA Tour rules and regulations."

However it is was only open to players who left the PGA Tour at least two years ago and have won the The Players Championship or one of the four majors. DeChambeau, Cam Smith and Rahm were, therefore, the only players that qualified. But with that door now seemingly closed even to them, a return looks complex.

"I'm not part of the discussions but I'm pretty sure they aren't going to be welcomed back straight away," said Rory McIlroy, a six-time major winner who has been consistently critical of LIV, in August.

"They were offered this returning member program back in February, the one Brooks [Koepka] took, but that has come and gone and I think it was said at the time that the deal they get going forward if they decide to come back would not be as good at the one Brooks got. So I'd say it will be a tough road back."

articles.title: DA seeks P300M to develop local palm oil sector
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agriculture (DA) is requesting P300 million in budget support for 2027 to develop the Philippine palm oil sector and cut import reliance. Agriculture Secretary…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agriculture (DA) is requesting P300 million in budget support for 2027 to develop the Philippine palm oil sector and cut import reliance.
Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. emphasized the need for funding to enhance local palm oil production for import substitution and cleaner fuel feedstock.
The agriculture chief likewise noted that the country imports 90 percent of its palm oil requirements.

“Definitely, palm oil is an industry that needs support from the national government and LGUs (local government units) that have palm oil industries or stakeholders in the area because our palm oil producers and farmers earn money and the market is already there,” Tiu Laurel said during a recent House of Representatives budget hearing.
Likewise, the agri chief proposed a P1 billion annual funding commitment for five years if Congress supports the sector.
Separately, the government plans to develop 300,000 hectares of palm oil plantations, aiming for 100,000 hectares by 2028 as a notable achievement.

“The expansion could eventually help develop a domestic source of palm oil that could be used not only for food and industrial applications but also as potential feedstock for cleaner fuel,” the DA said.
Meanwhile, Tiu Laurel stated that the agency didn’t include the budget request in its National Expenditure Program due to a recent awareness of the increased need for support.
In addition to funding support, Tiu Laurel is calling for a deputy administrator and teams at the PCA for palm oil and coconut development.

“What is important is that we can build an agency or organize the PCA not just as a coconut authority, but to have a deputy administrator specifically for palm oil and coconut so they have their own teams,” he added.
Additionally, Tiu Laurel said the DA will officially recommend to President Marcos that the proposed Palm Oil Bill be certified as urgent.
House Bill No. 7462 or the Philippine Palm Oil Development Act, seeks to expand oil palm plantations and enhance productivity and quality.
It aims to improve competitiveness, productivity, and efficiency in crude palm oil processing and promote government-private partnerships in the sector. /pai

articles.title: Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral
articles.summary: Heads of state from around the world came to Oslo to pay tribute to the late monarch.

image.caption: Harald reigned for 35 years, eschewing the modern tradition of abdicating in old ageImage: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP

blocks.text: A 21-gun salute rang out over Oslo on Wednesday afternoon as the coffin of Norway's King Harald V left the royal palace for the city's Lutheran cathedral.
Thousands of people lined the streets to say goodbye to the king.
Norway then observed a minute of silence to start the funeral service.
The procession and funeral will bring an end to 13 days of national mourning following the death of the well-liked and down-to-earth monarch at the age of 89.

blocks.caption: King Haakon (second from left) walked alongside his children and sisterImage: Ole Berg-Rusten/NTB/REUTERS

blocks.text: Who is attending the funeral?

The funeral is being attended by heads of state and government from all over the world. This includes the UK's Prince William and Princess Anne, Japan's Crown Prince Fumihito and his wife Princess Kiko, Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia, as well as fellow Scandinavian royals from Denmark and Sweden.
Other leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier are also attending.
Harald's son King Haakon VIII will be there alongside his mother Queen Sonja and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit.
Controversially, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship is also expected to be at the funeral.
Marius Borg Hoiby's participation in an earlier part of the official mourning drew an outcry in Norway, as he was recently convicted of rape and domestic violence and is under house arrest.

articles.title: Serbia dissolves parliament as snap elections called
articles.summary: Serbia will head to the polls in late October after President Aleksandar Vucic dissolved parliament following growing pressure from protesters demanding political change. However, Vucic plans to…

image.caption: Aleksandar Vucic has signaled his ambition to run for prime ministerImage: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic signed an order on Wednesday calling for an early election after dissolving parliament.
"Elections will be held in Serbia on October 25. I believe that, after the elections, we will finally emerge from this crisis," he said.
"We have had … huge turbulences," Vucic said in an televised address. "We need election results that will clearly show the will of the people and the direction where Serbia is going."
Since November 2024, student-led protests have demanded Vucic step down, alleging corruption ⁠and authoritarianism.
The protests emerged after the collapse of a railway station in the northern city of Novi Sad, which left at least 16 people dead. Protesters say corruption led to shoddy construction work.
Initial calls for a transparent investigation then turned into demands for snap elections.
Nationalist leader Vucic has held power as both president and prime minister for more than a decade.
He is not allowed to run for another presidential term, but he has said he plans to run for prime minister instead.
More to come...

articles.title: Electronic shelf labels likely to cost jobs and drive up grocery prices, US report warns
articles.summary:
AFL-CIO calls for ban on such labels to protect consumers and workers from surveillance pricing and job cuts

The universal adoption of electronic shelf labels in grocery stores across the US…

blocks.text: The universal adoption of electronic shelf labels in grocery stores across the US could cost tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in lost wages while further driving up grocery costs, according to a report released on Tuesday.

An analysis by the AFL-CIO Tech Institute of the label manufacturers’ own marketing materials found the universal adoption of electronic shelf labels, which are marketed to retailers as a cost-cutting measure, could cost workers between $1.6bn to $6.9bn in lost wages annually and affect between 44,223 and 191,633 jobs.
The policy brief – Priced Out, Pushed Out: Electronic Shelf Labels Raise Prices and Shrink Paychecks – calls for a ban on electronic labels to protect consumers and workers.
Manufacturers have hailed the labels as a way to collect massive amounts of personal data from customers, increase profits, and cut labor costs.

The report argues that electronic shelf labels use the same pricing systems that allow dynamic pricing – price changes such as increasing allergy medication prices when pollen counts are high – to surveillance pricing, changing prices based on personal data.
These technologies are being implemented across the US retail industry at a time when food prices have surpassed inflation and wage gains, increasing 33% over the past seven years.

“Through our analysis, we found that the implementation of electronic shelf labels are likely going to drive prices even higher. The reason being that these labels are connected to the same algorithmic pricing software that online retailers are already using,” said Sunny Glottmann, policy and programs managers at the AFL-CIO Tech Institute and co-author of the report.

“Electronic shelf labels create the infrastructure that would make rapid algorithmic price changes easier to implement at scale, and this raises concerns for consumers that are already struggling with grocery costs.”

The report comes as several states have begun introducing legislation to ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels. In April, Maryland became the first state in the US to ban surveillance pricing. Connecticut signed a ban into law in June and New Jersey signed a ban into law in July.
Electronic shelf labels “enable instantaneous price changes”, said Lauren McFerran, executive director of the AFL-CIO Tech Institute and former chairman of the National Labor Relations Board.

“This is a technology that both is enabling this kind of ‘how do we extract the absolute most money out of grocery shoppers that is humanly possible’ and ‘how do we squeeze our workers as much as is humanly possible’,” said McFerran.

A May poll released by the United Food and Commercial Workers union found 68% of Americans believe surveillance pricing will increase grocery costs and 65% say digital price tags will do the same. Some 67% support banning digital price tags and surveillance pricing, with only 26% opposing a ban.

Ademola Oyefeso, vice-president of UFCW International, said that as retailers are implementing electronic shelf labels, the labor cuts occur gradually, with workers who typically change prices on shelves losing work hours.

“Slowly, if someone has a full-time job or a part-time job, they go from full-time to part-time, from part-time to no time, and that’s what’s going to start happening across the entire industry,” said Oyefeso. “We have gone with paper labels for over 100 years. It’s worked. It’s the trust stores have built with people. I know [that] you and I are paying the same price.
“If we come there on Monday, you and I are going to pay the same price on Monday, on Tuesday, on Wednesday.”
Oyefeso said workers are also consumers, and that electronic shelf labels allowing price changes to occur multiple times a day.

In December, Instacart ended a pilot program practice that allowed retailers to charge online shoppers different prices for the same products after an investigation by Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found grocery prices could differ by as much as 23% between customers.
“ESLs are the embodiment of surge pricing and surveillance pricing,” Oyefeso said. “Shelf labels allow grocery shopping to become airline ticket shopping.”

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border
articles.summary: Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk.

blocks.text: Two people have been killed after Russian drones struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

The Starokozache crossing, around 500km (310 miles) south of Kyiv, was closed after the overnight attack. Images from the scene showed several cars left completely scorched, with wreckage and debris strewn across the border post.
Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk in a Ukrainian drone attack, the regional governor said.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up long-range strikes in recent months, despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Zelensky renewed calls for international support in the wake of the Starokozache crossing attack, saying "the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further".
The border link between Ukraine and Moldova was shut after the attack killed two people and injured three others, Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper said.
A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to the country's foreign ministry.

Moldova has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict, with Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirming that 17 drones had struck Moldovan territory in August alone - more than during the whole of last year.
"Those who ignore or downplay these threats - and refuse to name the aggressor - are denying reality," he wrote on social media.
"Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility."

articles.title: Win: Sara Duterte's impeachment trial verdict eyed before December
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin "Win" Gatchalian and other senators are eyeing to wrap up Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial before December, hoping that a verdict would be reached before the…

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 6:50pm

Senate President Sherwin "Win" Gatchalian and other senators are eyeing to wrap up Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial before December, hoping that a verdict would be reached before the year ends.
In an ambush interview at the Senate on Wednesday, Gatchalian said the prosecution's move to drop 15 witnesses has a big impact on the trial's timeline.
"Ang timetable na nakikita namin, hopefully, before December matapos na lahat," Gatchalian said.
(The timetable that we see, hopefully before December, everything is finished.)
Gatchalian stressed that this still depends on the witnesses that the defense will present after the prosecution is finished tackling all four Articles of Impeachment.
However, Gatchalian said the defense has already lessened the number of witnesses they planned to present.
Meanwhile, Senate finance committee chair Senator JV Ejercito said he wanted to get the trial done as soon as possible to allow more time for the budget hearings.

"Sana mapabilis na ito para makabalik na tayo sa normal na pamumuhay. Kasi dami nating kailangan ayusin. Daming problema. Nakaka-apekto rin siyempre 'yung hidwaan sa politika sa overall, sa lahat ng takbo natin ng bansa," Ejercito said.
(I hope the trial progresses faster so we can get back to normal. Because we have so many things to fix. A lot of problems. The political divide is affecting the way that the country is being run.)
The prosecution panel dropped the 15 witnesses in Article 1 of the Articles of Impeachment, hoping to replace them with Duterte instead. Article 1 refers to the alleged misuse of confidential funds.
Senators have previously lamented the prolonged time that the impeachment trial was taking away from other legislative matters. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Ministers to put white working-class people in UK at heart of new equalities unit
articles.summary: Bridget Phillipson to announce creation of unit which will make class a key part of its equalities agenda

blocks.text: The government is putting class at the heart of its equalities agenda by creating a new unit that will make tackling white working-class inequality a priority.

The unit, which the minister for women and equalities, Bridget Phillipson, will announce on Wednesday, will sit within the Office for Equality and Opportunity and examine disparities linked to class and socioeconomic background across all ethnic groups.
Improving outcomes for white working-class people will be a focus of its work, even though government sources insisted it would not be a dedicated white working-class unit.

It comes as part of a government shakeup of its equalities work that will result in the Social Mobility Commission being abolished. Social class will not, however, be given a new legal status as a protected characteristic under the Equality Act.
The unit will act as a centre for government analysis of class and socioeconomic inequalities in public services and outcomes.

One of its first priorities will be the introduction of the socioeconomic duty, which will force public bodies to consider how their decisions could reduce inequalities felt by lower income families, caused by socioeconomic disadvantages such as transport and services.
Phillipson is expected to announce plans to change the way deprivation is measured across the country, with an assessment on how funding is distributed across services such as childcare and health.
The new unit is being established as the Social Mobility Commission (SMC) is abolished. The SMC was established in 2010 to monitor progress on social mobility and advise ministers.
Government insiders are thought to believe the commission has not been effective enough in guiding policy, given it can only advise ministers when requested.
Some of the 20 civil servants who work in the Cabinet Office and supported the SCM’s work are expected to move to the new unit.

The SCM’s latest report, titled State of the Nation, says “entrenched disadvantages” lie in former industrial communities across Britain, which face “extreme regional differences”, fewer job opportunities and poorer childhoods.
An independent inquiry into white working-class educational outcomes found Britain’s education system was not “serving the interests of white working-class children”.

It also said high-performing primary and secondary schools in England should be encouraged to admit more disadvantaged pupils from white working-class backgrounds to help reverse a continuing crisis in underachievement.
At the time of its conclusion in June, Phillipson, the then education secretary, said “for the first time in a long time white working-class children have a government that will fight for them”.

She added that generations had been “robbed of opportunity” and “the communities in this report are my communities. I know what they’ve given this country and what this country has failed to give back.”

The inquiry was commissioned by Star Academies and supported by the Department for Education to understand why white working-class children were the lowest performing demographic in England’s school system.

The Sutton Trust educational charity warned at the time against setting one disadvantaged group against another, noting that disadvantaged young people from Black Caribbean backgrounds were just as unlikely to become top earners.

articles.title: House eyes Oct. 9 approval of P7.2T nat'l budget for 2027
articles.summary: The House of Representatives is expected to approve the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 on third and final reading by October 9, House appropriations panel vice chairperson and…

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 6:44pm

The House of Representatives is expected to approve the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 on third and final reading by October 9, House appropriations panel vice chairperson and Surigao del Sur Rep. Romeo Momo Sr. said Wednesday.

In a press briefing, Momo, who is said the timeline is feasible as the House Committee on Appropriations had already completed its panel-level deliberations on the proposed 2027 budgets of various government agencies on Tuesday, September 8.

“The last budget hearing concluded as planned yesterday. We are slated to begin plenary deliberations next week, and we remain on track to approve the House General Appropriations Bill, or GAB, on third reading by the end of the legislative calendar on October 9,” Momo added.

Also on Wednesday, Momo said House leaders are looking to increase the Department of Public Works and Highways’ proposed P643-billion budget for 2027, saying additional funding is needed to complete high-impact projects, including flood control projects.

“There are a lot of projects which need additional investment in the DPWH. These are projects with economic multipliers such as farm-to-market roads, national highways and bridges, as well as inter-provincial and inter-island connectivity projects for the movement of our people and goods,” Momo said.
He, however, did not specify how much the House intends to increase the DPWH’s proposed budget.
Momo made the disclosure amid an ongoing scandal over alleged irregularities in flood control projects, including accusations that lawmakers received kickbacks from public works contracts.
He said the House would prioritize the completion of ongoing flood control projects that are backed by master plans and feasibility studies, particularly those in areas at high risk of flooding.

“At the same time, we also need to address the needs of our communities such as health care centers, evacuation centers, and flood control projects. If the flood control project is in accordance with a master plan, a feasibility study and its construction is already underway, those need to be completed first to be effective," he said.
"We will prioritize those in high-risk areas for flooding. Rest assured that the projects that will be funded are only those we need,” Momo added.
The DPWH already ranks second among the top 10 agencies with the highest budget allocations, next to the Department of Education (DepEd), which has a proposed P976-billion budget.

Other agencies among the 10 biggest recipients are the Department of Health, Department of the Interior and Local Government, Department of National Defense, Department of Transportation, Department of Agriculture, Department of Social Welfare and Development, Commission on Higher Education and state universities and colleges.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: SC acquits Imelda Marcos in graft case over Swiss foundations
articles.summary: The Supreme Court has overturned former First Lady Imelda Marcos" graft conviction over her alleged financial interests in seven Swiss foundations.

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 6:43pm
The Supreme Court has overturned former First Lady Imelda Marcos’ graft conviction over her alleged financial interests in seven Swiss foundations.
In a decision dated June 10, 2026, but made public on Wednesday, September 9, the SC First Division reversed the Sandiganbayan’s November 2018 ruling that found her guilty of seven counts of graft.

Marcos allegedly had pecuniary interests and participation in the management of several non-government organizations in Switzerland from 1978 to 1984 during her time as Minister of Human Settlements, Metro Manila Governor, and interim member of the Batasan Pambansa.

The Sandiganbayan said the seven foundations-Maler Establishment, Trinidad Foundation, Rayby Foundation, Palmy Foundation, Vibur Foundation, Aguamina Foundation, and Avertina Foundation - were established primarily to benefit the Marcos family.

It said that the foundations were "put up primarily for the entrepreneurial activity of opening bank accounts and deposits, transferring funds, earning interests and even profit from investment, for the private benefit of the Marcos family as beneficiaries."
Acting on Marcos' appeal, the SC found the prosecution’s testimonial and documentary evidence inadmissible and lacking in probative value.

"In sum, the relevant Swiss documents were not properly authenticated. The prosecution was not able to present any credible witness who could have attested to the genuineness and due execution of the documents," the SC said through Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda.

"All told, the prosecution failed to establish that the subject foundations are businesses as the term is ordinarily understood. Any financial or pecuniary interest in the subject foundations is not covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution. Doubts on the coverage of the term 'business' should be resolved against the State and in favor of the accused-appellant," it said. — VBL, GMA News

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) 1st Division acquitted Imelda Marcos, the mother of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., in her graft cases related to Swiss foundations.
In a decision made public on Wednesday, September 9, the SC division overturned the Sandiganbayan’s November 2018 decision that convicted the 97-year-old former first lady of seven counts of graft.

“Accordingly, the Appeal is granted. The November 9, 2018 Decision of the Sandiganbayan in Criminal Case Nos. 17287, 17288, 17289, 17290, 22867, 22868, and 22869 is reversed and set aside. Accused-appellant Imelda R. Marcos is acquitted for the prosecution’s failure to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt for violation of Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019, in relation to Article IX, Section 8 of the 1973 Constitution,” said the 50-page ruling penned by Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda.
Associate justices Ramon Paul Hernando, Henri Jean Paul Inting, Ricardo Rosario, and Jose Midas Marquez all concurred in the ruling.
The Marcos matriarch is acquitted four years into the presidential term of her son, who won the presidency in 2022.
In its decision, the SC division said the prosecution failed to prove Marcos’ guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Beyond reasonable doubt is the threshold needed to convict an accused in criminal cases.
Marcos was charged with alleged violation of Section 3(h), which has the following elements:

items: the accused is a public officer
they have direct or indirect financial or pecuniary interest in any business, contract, or transaction
they either intervened or took part in their official capacity or connection with such interest, or they are prohibited from having such interest by the Constitution or by any law

blocks.text: The SC said it’s undisputed that the first element is present, but the second and third elements are contested. The Office of the Ombudsman presented documentary and testimonial evidence that sought to prove Marcos’ financial interest, but the SC said they were “inadmissible and lack probative weight.”

In Marcos’ case, the Sandiganbayan found that she had a financial and pecuniary interest in the foundations based on the Swiss documents. The documents were retrieved from Swiss banks and had been authenticated in accordance with Swiss legal procedure.
However, the SC said the Sandiganbayan erred when it considered the Swiss documents duly authenticated.

“The Court has emphasized that the rule on authentication, more particularly as to private documents, is in place to prevent the inclusion of spurious documents in the body of evidence. Thus, it is settled that private documents are generally inadmissible in evidence unless they are properly authenticated,” said the ruling, adding that the prosecution was not able to present a credible witness who could have testified to the documents’ authenticity.

In addition, even if the SC would ignore the probative weight of the prosecution’s evidence, Marcos must still be acquitted, said the Court. The prosecution, according to the SC, failed to prove that the alleged pecuniary interest was “covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution.”

“All told, the prosecution failed to establish that the subject foundations are businesses as the term is ordinarily understood. Any financial or pecuniary interest in the subject foundations is not covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution. Doubts on the coverage of the term ‘business’ should be resolved against the State and in favor of the accused-appellant,” said the ruling. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Republicans put Trump center stage for convention in US midterms gamble
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump is due to address Republicans tonight at the party’s first ever national convention ahead of the crucial midterm elections, with the GOP hoping to energize voters as it fights to hold its narrow congressional majorities.
The two-day gathering takes place in Dallas, marking a break from the longstanding tradition of holding national conventions only during presidential election years.
“It has never been done before, and will be a truly Historic Event,” Trump said in July while announcing the convention, promising the convention would feature “Great Entertainment”.
Trump first floated the idea for a convention last year, arguing that it would provide an opportunity to showcase his administration’s achievements since he returned to the White House in 2024.
More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.

Trump delivers this evening’s keynote speech and returns for Thursday’s finale after vice-president JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program.
Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left.

blocks.text: Trump gave $45,000 to Natalie Harp and other White House aides as holiday gifts
Donald Trump gave sizable holiday gifts to four White House aides, according to new financial disclosures released by the administration, including $45,000 to executive assistant Natalie Harp.

Communications adviser Margo Martin and deputy director of Oval Office operations Chamberlain Harris also received $45,000, while director of Oval Office operations Walt Nauta received a $20,000 gift.

The gifts were noted in the staffers’ annual financial disclosure forms that were published by the administration last week. Harp, Martin and Harris make $150,000 annually and Nauta is paid $175,000 a year, according to the White House’s salary disclosure report to Congress.

A White House official told the Associated Press that Trump “has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector.”

The official did not say if any other staffers were given similar gifts from the president, but added that the cash gifts were not related to the “individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards.”
The disclosures of the gifts were first reported earlier on Tuesday by The Washington Post.
