articles.title: Policeman kills teacher wife at Thai school, kids safe: officials
articles.summary: BANGKOK, Thailand – A police officer shot dead his teacher wife at the kindergarten where she worked in Thailand on Wednesday but all the children are safe, officials said. The gunman returned…

blocks.text: BANGKOK, Thailand – A police officer shot dead his teacher wife at the kindergarten where she worked in Thailand on Wednesday but all the children are safe, officials said.
The gunman returned home after the shooting in Chonburi province, southeast of Bangkok, where police were negotiating his surrender.
The incident is the latest shooting to rock Thailand, a month after a teenager shot his grandparents and then five staff and a pupil at his school, before killing himself.
Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region, and past promises of tightening gun laws have not prevented repeated shootings.

Sayan Klomaon, chairman of Nong Pla Lai sub-district council, told AFP the gunman — a policeman local to the area — came to the school at about 10:30 am (0330 GMT) and talked with his wife before shooting her.
No students saw the incident, as it happened outside the classroom, he said, adding that the gunman then left to go home, and since then all the children had been picked up.
In a statement on Facebook, Chonburi Governor Naris Niramaiwong confirmed that all 44 children were safely evacuated along with three teachers and three other staff members.
He said police had surrounded the house where the gunman was and were negotiating his surrender.
The motive remains unclear.
Naris ordered the kindergarten closed and said psychological support will be provided to children and staff who witnessed the incident.
In 2022, an ex-policeman armed with a gun and a knife stormed a nursery in northern Thailand and killed 24 children and 12 adults, in one of the country’s deadliest massacres.

articles.title: Palace rejects claim that Marcos betrayed Romualdez
articles.summary: Malacañang on Wednesday rejected the claim that President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. betrayed his cousin, former speaker and Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez, following the…

blocks.text: Malacañang on Wednesday rejected the claim that President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. betrayed his cousin, former speaker and Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez, following the latter's arrest on plunder charges over the flood control corruption scandal.

Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Atty. Claire Castro said this in a Palace briefing when asked for a comment that Marcos seemingly turned his back on his cousin—known to be his erstwhile staunch ally—to face the charges against him.

"Hindi ko gusto ang word na 'nilaglag.' So kung may mga kritikong nagsasabing nilaglag, hindi namin nais gamitin ang word na nilaglag," Castro said in response to a question regarding criticisms on social media that the President threw his cousin under the bus.
(I don't like the word 'nilaglag.' So, if there are critics saying that, we do not wish to use that word.)

"Dahil ito naman po, according to the Office of the Ombudsman, mayroon silang nakitang ebidensya. So walang dapat nilalaglag dito. Kung ano lang ang ebidensya na nandiyan, doon lang tayo bumase," she added.
(In this case, according to the Office of the Ombudsman, they found evidence. So, there is no one being dropped here. We should simply base our actions on evidence.)
Castro also maintained that the President is "neutral" and respects the processes under the law.
Citing the Office of the Ombudsman, she also said a number of pending cases are still under investigation against other individuals in relation to the flood control mess.

Romualdez was arrested on Monday at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, the same day that the Office of the Ombudsman filed a P7.4-billion plunder charge against him and three others over their alleged involvement in flood control project kickbacks.
The former speaker sought the approval of the Sandiganbayan Third Division to grant him "continued hospital confinement" as he faces his plunder case.

In a nine-page manifestation addressed to the Sandiganbayan, Romualdez said that he was admitted to the hospital on September 7, 2026, citing his medical history that included issues with his cardiovascular and brain condition.
Hospital detention
Castro also distanced the President from discussions on whether Romualdez will be allowed to remain under hospital detention following his arrest.

"Sa ngayon walang pinag-uusapan tungkol sa hospital arrest. Depende na po kasi 'yan kung ano ang magiging findings ng doktor at mas nanaisin po natin kung ang magbibigay ng suhestiyon na ito ay masasabi nating hindi kaugnay kay Speaker Romualdez," she said.

(As of now, there are no discussions regarding the hospital arrest. That will depend on the doctor's findings, and we would prefer that the person making the recommendation be someone who is not linked to speaker Romualdez.)

"Kumbaga neutral, ang kanyang findings ay neutral. So depende na po 'yan sa doktor. Hiindi 'yan panghihimasukan ng administration at hindi po natin masasaklawan kung anong pakiramdam, health condition ng sino mang akusado," she added.

(The person giving the findings should be neutral. So, that is up to the doctor. The administration will not interfere with that, and we cannot dictate the health condition or how any accused individual is feeling.)
The Philippine National Police (PNP) has prepared a room for Romualdez in case he is allowed to remain under hospital detention following his arrest on plunder charges.
However, the Office of the Ombudsman stood firm that it would "strongly oppose" Romualdez's bid for hospital detention.
Will Marcos visit?
Castro also said she has no information whether Marcos intends to visit Romualdez in the hospital.
She said how the President personally feels about the situation need not be aired in public.
"Ang pakiramdam po ng Pangulo personal ay hindi naman po siguro ito dapat nang alamin natin. Ang kailangan lang po dito ay dapat mapanagot ang dapat na mapanagot," Castro said.
(The President's feelings on the matter are personal. We don't need to pry into those. What matters is that those who need to be held accountable are held accountable.)

"Hindi na po siguro makakaapekto kung ano man ang damdamin ng Pangulo—masaya, malungkot, anuman, hindi na po siya importante. Ang importante po dito ay gumagana ang ating hustisya at kung kailangan na siya ay (masingil) kung mayroon man dahilan at ito ay makikita sa korte, hayaan na po natin ang korte na siyang humusga sa kasong ito," she continued.

(Whatever the President feels—whether happy, sad, or otherwise—it doesn't matter. What's important is that our justice system is working. If there are grounds to hold someone liable, and if this is something to be determined in court, let's just leave that to the court.) — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: House leaders eye increasing DPWH's proposed P643-B budget for 2027
articles.summary: House leaders on Wednesday said they will look to increase the Department of Public Works and Highways" proposed P643-billion budget for 2027, saying such increase is needed to complete high impact…

blocks.text: House leaders on Wednesday said they will look to increase the Department of Public Works and Highways’ proposed P643-billion budget for 2027, saying such increase is needed to complete high impact projects, including flood control projects.

“There are a lot of projects which need additional investment in the DPWH. These are projects with economic multipliers such as farm-to-market roads, national highways and bridges, as well as inter-provincial and inter-island connectivity projects for the movement of our people and goods,” Surigao del Sur Representative Romeo Momo, chairperson of the House public works and highways panel, said at a press conference.

“At the same time, we also need to address the needs of our communities such as health care centers, evacuation centers, and flood control projects. If the flood control project is in accordance with a master plan, a feasibility study and its construction is already underway, those need to be completed first to be effective. We will prioritize those in high-risk areas for flooding. Rest assured that the projects that will be funded are only those we need,” Momo added.

Momo said such requirements of a meritorious DPWH project include a Certificate of Implementability, Program of Work, geotagged project-site documentation, appropriate local sanggunian resolutions, among others.

Quezon Representative Reynante Arrogancia, vice chairperson of the House appropriations panel, said the additional budget for DPWH will likely come from realignment of allocations under the Department of Transportation, Department of Agriculture, National Irrigation Authority, as well as the Department of Information and Communications Technology and the Metro Manila Development Authority.

“We’ll look at their utilitization rate of their respective budget allocation. Kung hindi nila nagagamit ang lahat ng pondo, ibig sabihin kailangan natin itong irealign o gamitin muna sa ibang agency, para magamit ng DPWH o iba pang anumang purpose,” Arrogancia said.
(If they are not able to use their budget, it must be realigned to other agencies such as the DPWH for its perusal.)

Momo, for his part, said such realignment will only involve agencies that also implement infrastructure projects so as not to compromise other vital government programs such as education and healthcare.

“The realigned funds to the DPWH will only come from agencies implementing infrastructure projects. Rest assured that nothing that goes to DPWH will be taken away from education, health, and social services. Hindi gagalawin iyon,” Momo said.
(Allocations for those sectors won't be touched.)
“We are only going to realign the funds from agencies which, historically, do not have good absorptive capacity rating in implementing infrastructure projects,” Momo added.
Zero budget for public transport items

Earlier, House Assistant Minority Leader Perci Cendaña of Akbayan flagged the zero allocation for the NCR Busway Project (which includes the EDSA Busway), Service Contracting Program, and the Fuel Subsidy Program under the Department of Transportation’s (DOTr) proposed 2027 budget.

“The national budget is the ultimate expression of the President’s priorities and commitments. Kapag malaki ang budget sa isang programa, mataas ang priority. Kapag walang budget, hindi ka priority. Pinapakita lang nitong zero budget na hindi priority ang milyon-milyong commuters at ang libu-libong tsuper at transport workers," Cendaña said in a statement.

(When a program has a huge budget, it is high priority. But if there is zero budget, that projects is not a priority. The zero allocation for these projects means that this government do not see the commuters, drivers and other public transport workers as a priority.)
The Akbayan lawmaker then warned that removing funding for the programs could worsen the daily commute for millions of Filipinos while increasing the financial burden on public transport workers.

“The NCR/EDSA Busway has provided millions of commuters with a faster and more reliable way to get to work, school, and home. Service contracting has helped keep public transport running while supporting drivers and operators especially during times of crises. Fuel subsidies, meanwhile, provide much-needed relief to drivers struggling with fuel price shocks caused by the war in the Middle East. Nakakalungkot naman na kapag usapin ng pagtitipid, ’yung kapakanan ng ating commuters at public transport workers ang tinitipid," Cendaña said.

"These are not luxuries. These are essential public transport programs that directly affect the daily lives and livelihoods of millions of Filipinos. I hope our colleagues in the House will join us in pushing to restore the requested budgets of these programs," Cendaña added. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
articles.summary: Traffickers are making big bucks smuggling millions of critically endangered eels across continents, in suitcases on planes or by exploiting legal loopholes to end up on dinnerplates. Where are the…

image.caption: Unai Eizaguirre, an eel fisherman for 30 years, prepares gear with a colleague in the Basque CountryImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades.

The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels.

"So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous."

Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed.
"I don't know if the eel has time to wait for these projects to show their effects," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI.

blocks.caption: Marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says only 12% of eels now survive the journey from the Sargasso SeaImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs

Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels."

Today, only about 12% survive the journey from the Sargasso to the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways, Diaz told DW. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9000 ($10,400) per kilogram.

"You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel.

Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: so far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market.

Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years.

"Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate."
International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025.
"There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes."

blocks.caption: A small dam near Plentzia — obstacles like this can block eels on their migration routeImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: Eels smuggled in plain sight in regular suitcases along complex routes

Still, Stein, who did his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex.
"Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he said. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal.

Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important.

Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW.

European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe.

From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms.

blocks.caption: In Plentzia, where eel fishing has long been part of daily life, fishermen say the regional ban risks hurting those who follow the rules while illegal traders continue to profitImage: Nicole Ris/DW

blocks.text: A species running out of time

Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish.
"But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz.

Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea.

But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key.

"The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban.

“The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future.

Baby orangutans rescued, sparking international smuggling probe
Indian forest officials rescued five baby orangutans in the eastern state of Odisha on Tuesday, with authorities suspecting the great apes were smuggled into the country from Southeast Asia.

The animals, not native to India, were found in a forest in the Balasore district. Local legislator Goutam Buddha Das told The Telegraph newspaper that villagers first spotted the orangutans dangling from a tree and initially mistook them for monkeys, before alerting forest officials that their appearance didn't match.
He said the area's coastal location suggested the animals could have arrived by sea from Indonesia.
"I demand a high-level inquiry to find out who is involved in the racket," Das said.

Balasore forest officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar said the three male and two female orangutans were examined by veterinarians, found to be in good health, and given food and oral rehydration solution before being transferred to Nandan Kanan Zoo in Bhubaneswar for quarantine.
Odisha Environment Minister Ram Singh Khuntia said the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau is now investigating how the animals reached India.
"We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this," he told the IANS news agency. Authorities are also examining whether the animals were destined for sale to buyers in Kolkata.
Orangutans are native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra. Only about 104,000 remain in the wild, according to the World Wildlife Fund, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
Borneo's orangutans fight to survive
The Tapanuli orangutan is critically endangered, with fewer than 800 animals thought to be left.

articles.title: Tulfo on China’s note to Teodoro: ‘They shouldn’t have done that’
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Erwin Tulfo has criticized the Chinese delegate who passed a note to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. while he was speaking at the Seoul Defense Dialogue, saying that…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Erwin Tulfo has criticized the Chinese delegate who passed a note to Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. while he was speaking at the Seoul Defense Dialogue, saying that it was improper.

Tulfo on Wednesday was referring to the incident in which Teodoro was handed a note supposedly from a Chinese military attaché at the Chinese Embassy in Seoul while discussing the importance of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) at the forum on Tuesday.
The note dismissed the South China Sea arbitration, calling the 2016 award “illegal, null, and void.”
“They shouldn’t have done that,” Tulfo told the media in an ambush interview.
According to Tulfo, Teodoro’s response to the note was commendable, saying that if he were in Teodoro’s position, he might have gotten into trouble.
“That’s the right thing to do,” Tulfo said. “If I were handed that note, there might have been a problem… They might say it’s not something a senator should do, but I will really stand up.”
Upon receiving the note at the forum, Teodoro read portions of the message aloud, reacting in between.
When the message disregarded the Unclos decision, Teodoro pointed out that even China had signed the international framework.
The note also reiterated that China does not recognize the 2016 ruling. To this, Teodoro said, “Of course, because you lost.”
Teodoro also denounced the act of passing him a note in the middle of the forum, saying it was disrespectful to the organizers and guests, adding that China needs “basic decency and behavior.”
He also called the note “actual coercion, bullying and aggression,” which is a reminder of “China’s weak position.”
The audience at the forum applauded Teodoro afterward. /mcm

articles.title: Trafficked into fraud: An African crisis situation in Cambodia
articles.summary: Cambodia is cracking down on scam operators, with the effects being felt mostly among young Africans: Thousands of trafficking victims are now stuck in the Asian country with no money, no passport,…

image.caption: Many of the Africans trafficked to Cambodia are lured there with false promisesImage: DW

blocks.text: Southeast Asia has long emerged as a major hub of highly organized online fraud operations, targeting people all around the world.

According to the United Nations, these operations generate tens of billions of dollars annually, having long surpassed the illegal drug trade as the most profitable activity for criminal networks, as reported by the United States Institute of Peace.

However, those who fall prey to scams and other fraudulent activities aren't the only victims of these criminal rings; the scam industry in Southeast Asia alone is powered by at least 300,000 trafficked workers from 66 countries, who are routinely subjected to torture, sexual abuse, and forced labor, according to a recent UN Human Rights report.
Dream job abroad? It could be a trafficking trap

African nationals now form the largest group of those trafficked to and stranded in countries like Myanmar and Cambodia, without any viable pathway to go back home, says the NGO Freedom Collaborative.
In Cambodia, one of the main obstacles for facilitating any return is the fact that many African countries like Uganda, Liberia, Ghana, of Nigeria have no consular representation.
"But also because some countries have zero interest," says Montse Ferrer, co-regional director of Amnesty International, who finds equal blame for the situation in many of the countries of origin.
"They're not even picking up the phone, let alone providing the paperwork for the money for them to go back."
Cambodia's reluctant crackdown on scam operators
Ferrer believes that keeping the situation unchanged has also been in the interest of the Cambodian government for a long time:
Many trafficking victims now have overstay fines for their visas against their names in Cambodia, reaching thousands of dollars in many instances.
"They don't allow NGOs to provide the support these people need, and instead they have resorted to arresting and threatening them," Ferrer told DW.

Following great pressure from the international community — including threats of financial sanctions by the US, the UK, Canada and the European Union — Cambodia did eventually agree to launch a crackdown on the scamming industry earlier this year.
According to the Cambodian Ministry of Information, the initiative resulted in many arrests and triggered a mass exodus of dubious operatives from scamming industry.
Inside Cambodia's scam industry

But the crackdown also created a secondary crisis: Thousands of trafficked foreign workers remain stranded in the country without documentation nor legal status; now, they also lack shelter and money in many instances, NGOs say.
Many who have sought in Cambodia help have reportedly been placed in immigration detention, while others have to sleep rough and beg for food.
Instead of being given protection, many of the trafficking often victims now face stigmatization and abuse on the street of the capital Phnom Penh and elsewhere.

blocks.caption: Officials in Southeast Asia have been cracking down on scam factories, often conducting raids across bordersImage: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

blocks.text: Lured to Cambodia under false pretenses
Emmanuel David is one of many of the trafficking victims stuck in Cambodia. The 28-year-old Liberian national arrived there last year after a treacherous irregular journey originating in Vietnam.
"My friend told me there was work in Cambodia, but he did not explain that it was scamming work," David explained.

The scamming company had offered him a lucrative deal of making around $800 (€700) per month, which is more than double the average wage for qualified individuals in Liberia, according to the Civil Service Agency of Liberia.
The reality hit quite differently: Once there, he was forced to work 14 hours a day to deceive women on various dating apps to part with their money.
But David was initially unable — and later unwilling — to meet the set target quota of scams per day.
In response, the criminal group he worked for started billing him for food and accommodation through his wages, and later even confiscated his belongings — including his passport.
David says he also faced substantial physical violence, including beatings, for four months.
Eventually, he left "with no documents and no money," and is now hoping to find a way back to Liberia.
His story, however, is far from unique.
'Hundreds' of Africans trafficked to criminal compounds
Another survivor, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation, also recounted how he was "beaten and [subjected to] electric shocks."
The abuse resulted in him having to be hospitalized for three weeks, and is now unable to pay his medical bills.
Pia Oberoi, chief of the Right to Development Section at UN Human Rights, told DW that "despite the promise of a good salary, most come out in debt."

She also confirmed that more and more of the trafficking victims in Southeast Asia come from African countries, "because there is clearly a recruitment industry that's built around Africa, targeting African nationals."
Kenya scammers lured abroad
Other victims have corroborated this development, describing hundreds of Africans packed into heavily fortified compounds.
"Once you're inside there's no way out," an informant, who also chose to remain anonymous, told DW.
He said the compounds have their own laws, and that sexual abuse and psychological violence are an integral part of how they operate.
The police, he says, just turns a blind eye — at best.
No government assistance from any direction
Amnesty International speaks of an unfolding humanitarian crisis, warning that escapees are widely being treated as criminals rather than as trafficking victims.
"They shouldn't be punished for crimes they were forced to commit," Oberoi highlights, though her pleas appear to land on deaf ears.
Several of the victims contacted by DW said their governments were "slow" to help with their repatriation.
DW attempted to contact several African foreign ministries to hear their side, but has not received any response.

A statement issued by the Cambodian government meanwhile said that more than 700 compounds run chiefly by Chinese nationals had been raided, with 58,266 foreign nationals deported and nearly 30,000 suspects arrested over the past year.
However, the Cambodian government did not reply to DW's direct request for further information.

The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) meanwhile said it's trying its utmost to help the trafficking victims; but in the face of severe budgetary constraints, it can only provide "limited, prioritized support."
Fear, guilt and stigma
Humanitarian groups also warn of a high risk of victims being re-trafficked, even for those who have managed to return to their countries of origin.
In some instances, those who come back home are stigmatized as a failure — "a situation that is really unbearable," says Ferrer.
Emmanuel David is a prime example: He feels obliged to to apologize to his family for not returning a success. When asked about his little daughter, he says that "daddy can't go home without money."
To his mind, he hardly is the victim of his circumstances.

articles.title: Tycoon to pay ex-wife $1.87bn in record South Korea divorce settlement
articles.summary: The billion dollar payout marks the largest divorce settlement in the country's history.

blocks.text: A South Korean court has ordered gaming tycoon Kwon Hyuk-bin to pay his ex-wife 2.55tr won ($1.87bn; £1.38bn) in assets, marking the largest divorce settlement in the country's history.
Kwon, who founded South Korea's third-largest video game company Smilegate, is one of the country's richest men. Bloomberg puts his net worth at $3bn.

Smilegate was wholly owned by him until Wednesday when a court ruled that a 35% stake, valued at about 2.5tr won, be transferred to his wife Lee Hwa-jin. He was also ordered to pay her an additional 65bn won in cash.
This settlement is more than double the previous record of 944bn won which tech titan Chey Tae-won was ordered to pay his ex-wife.
In filing for divorce with Kwon, Lee had sought a 50% stake in Smilegate. Her lawyers argued that she had helped finance the company at its founding, according to Bloomberg.
Kwon and Lee got married in 2001, a year before he founded Smilegate. Its best-known titles include the first-person shooter game CrossFire and the action role-playing game Lost Ark.
Lee also said she spent more than 20 years raising their children and caring for their household.
Kwon in turn argued that Lee neither invested nor worked for the company. Earlier this year, Smilegate published a statement saying all of the company's initial capital came from Kwon.
A Smilegate spokesperson declined to "comment on the major shareholder's personal matters".
"We will continue to faithfully perform our duties as usual," they said in a statement cited by The Chosun Daily.
Both parties can still challenge the ruling.

In July this year, Chey Tae-won, the chairman of the corporate giant SK Group, was ordered to pay his ex-wife 944bn won which, prior to today's ruling, was the largest divorce award in Korean history.
However, this was later struck down by the Supreme Court who cited a miscalculation that increased the value of the couple's assets. It has ordered the case to be reviewed.

articles.title: Ukraine, Russia trade drone strikes, killing 6
articles.summary: At least four people were killed, and 29 others were injured, in a Ukrainian attack on a Russian Black Sea port. Meanwhile, Russian drones struck a crossing on the Ukraine-Moldova border, killing two.

image.caption: Traffic through the Starokozace crossing between Ukraine and Moldova was haltedImage: OdeskaODA/Telegram

blocks.text: A Ukrainian drone attack on the Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk overnight killed at least four people, including a child, Russian officials said Wednesday.
Veniamin Kondratyev, the governor of the Krasnodar region in southern Russia, said 29 others were injured in the drone attack.
Ukraine has frequently targeted Novorossiysk, a port city that is a major outlet for Russian oil and grain exports.
Earlier on Wednesday, the mayor of the city, Andrei Kravchenko, had said the debris from a Ukrainian drone fell onto several businesses and nearly landed on a residential building, sparking fires.
In the nearby town of Anapa, falling drone debris damaged three homes and a kindergarten, Kondratyev said, adding that there were no casualties.
Russia's Defense Ministry said nearly 600 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight.
Two civilians killed in Russian attack on border crossing
Russian drone strikes overnight on a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, meanwhile, killed at least two civilians, the regional governor Oleh Kiper said on social media.
Three people were wounded in the strike on the Starokozace border crossing, around 500 kilometres (310 miles) south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said.
The strikes forced the checkpoint to close temporarily, Kiper said, adding that multiple fires broke out as a result of the attack.
Ukrainian emergency officials also said the capital, Kyiv was attacked overnight. While some fires were started, there were no casualties.

blocks.caption: Russia's drone attack damaged a passenger bus and started fires, Ukraine saidImage: OdeskaODA/Telegram

blocks.text: What is the latest in US-brokered peace talks?
Russia on Tuesday resumed its near-daily airstrikes on Kyiv after a brief pause while US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow for talks.
At least five people were killed in Kyiv on Tuesday, officials said.

Russia also said President Vladimir Putin had had an "extremely frank" phone call with his US counterpart Donald Trump on Tuesday, as Washington continues to press Ukrainian and Russian officials to hold face-to-face talks to end the war.
Ukraine has suggested talks that could take place in September, but Russian officials have said it is "too early" to discuss specifics such as a venue or dates for the talks.
Despite US pressure, talks between Moscow and Kyiv have yielded no results beyond sporadic prisoner swaps.

September 9, 2026
Merz hits back at AfD after Saxony-Anhalt vote

blocks.caption: Merz said the far-right AfD remains a 'destructive force' in German politics Image: John Macdougall/AFP

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the German parliament, the Bundestag, gave a barbed response to opening remarks from the far-right Alternative for Germany's (AfD) co-leader Alice Weider, who lambasted Germany's ruling coalition as a "failure."
The Bundestag debate comes days after the AfD's after its strong showing in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, warning the party against assuming it was on course for broader majorities.

"Ms Weidel, today you can barely contain yourself," Merz told AfD co-leader Alice Weidel during the Bundestag's general debate on Wednesday. "But you do not have an absolute majority, and you will not achieve one in Germany."
"Nowhere in Germany will you win majorities with this politics," Merz said. "You are, and you remain a destructive force."
Merz acknowledged that the AfD had achieved "a remarkable election result in every respect" in Saxony-Anhalt.
"The voters spoke pretty clearly. They also sent us, and me personally, a clear message," he said.
However, he stressed that the AfD had failed to achieve its stated goal of securing an absolute majority in the state parliament in Magdeburg.
Merz accused the AfD of showing "contempt for our democratic institutions" and of repeatedly denigrating representatives of the state.
"You are and will remain a destructive force," Merz said.

blocks.caption: Merz's address was interrupted several times by the AfD faction Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: He said there was a "deep divide" between the AfD and the other parties in foreign, European, social and peace policy.
Merz also accused the AfD of damaging German interests through its friendly stance towards Russia.
"The only thing that really threatens Russia and Putin is the appeal of democracy," he said. "And yet you are obviously still standing on Russia's side."
"You are part of the problem we have in Germany — and we will resist that with everything at our disposal."

articles.title: Family of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigators
articles.summary:
Andrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in January

The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in…

blocks.text: The family of a British father who was found dead in the Caribbean in January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death.

Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at in Grenada on 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide.

In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”.
After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out.
The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”.
At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death.

The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”.
In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick.

“We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said.

It added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him.

“Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.”

Earlier this year, the family had called for an urgent review of the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation.

“Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said.

It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered.

“We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.”
In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”.
A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January.
“Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers.
“No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.”
Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force (RGPF) to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed.
Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations.

articles.title: Vietnamese firm targets Canadians with fake AI news for profit, CBC/Rad-Can investigation reveals
articles.summary: An investigation by CBC's visual investigations team and Radio-Canada's Décrypteurs has discovered a Vietnamese company is linked to a network of Facebook pages and websites sharing misleading,…
articles.byline: Eric Szeto, Jeff Yates, Christian Paas-Lang, Jordan Pearson, Ivan Angelovski

image.caption: A CBC/Radio-Canada investigation found hundreds of Facebook pages and website creating misleading and fake content originating from Vietnam. (Illustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; Juana Gibbs/YouTube, Life is Colorful/Facebook)

blocks.text: During a corporate party with dancing mascots and pyrotechnics in early 2026, the CEO of HTV Network stood on stage holding a sign in Vietnamese that said "Doanh Thu Đột Phá." Translation: "Record Revenue."

The CEO, Ngo Anh Tan, had reason to celebrate that night. Since launching as an "international media company" that connects the "world with authoritative journalism" almost two years earlier, HTV now had at least 100 employees, according to a Vietnamese job listing.
But what the company purports to do contrasts vastly with its true nature, an investigation by CBC’s visual investigations unit and Radio-Canada’s Décrypteurs discovered.
Exposing a Vietnamese AI fake news empire targeting Canadians

Ngo and his team secretly run an AI-slop empire out of Hanoi, Vietnam, polluting social media feeds around the world, targeting users with fake content and sensationalist stories that range from Elon Musk banning Teslas in Canada to clickbait-style posts exploiting the Tumbler Ridge shooting.

The team uncovered close to 200 Facebook pages — with more than 55 million followers — that shared links to about 50 HTV-connected websites that generate revenue by running ads, often next to inflammatory or misleading political and religious content.
"It's quite staggering, the scope of what's being done here," said Fenwick McKelvey, a professor specializing in communications at Concordia University in Montreal. "[It’s] totally deceptive."
HTV Network shares a name with a legitimate, state-owned Vietnamese broadcaster, complicating efforts to trace its activities.
'Everyone wins except for Canadians'

The model was relatively simple: The company mass-produced AI-generated content — showing, for example, how the "U.S. lost its main city" in an attack by Russian President Vladimir Putin — posted it on one of the Facebook pages they ran and included a hyperlink.

That link would take users to one of HTV's many websites, where ads for things like fungus medication, Bank of Montreal or Nova Scotia tourism would be plastered across the articles. Ads on websites viewed by CBC were served through third-party platforms, not the companies themselves.
The CBC/Radio-Canada analysis revealed that in some cases, the Facebook pages were also monetized.

HTV CEO Ngo, through text messages, told CBC/Radio-Canada he didn’t have Facebook pages or websites. When asked why his phone number matched the one on the HTV website, he said "maybe someone has taken my information." Corporate records and domain registration documentation also matched Ngo’s personal information.
Ngo repeatedly denied knowledge of HTV sites or pages. In response to a written request for comment, Ngo replied, "I don’t understand what you mean."

The following day, the HTV company website was taken down. Ngo's Facebook profile was made private and many of the digital clues CBC/Radio-Canada used to connect the company to the accounts and websites disappeared.
Aengus Bridgman, director of the Media Ecosystem Observatory, a joint McGill-University of Toronto project, said that Facebook incentivizes this kind of low-quality, clickable content.
Meta, Facebook’s parent company, recently invited users to join its creator program, where money can be made from reels, photos and text posts.

"The way this gets resolved is that there is some cost to Meta for enabling this sort of scam, a real concrete cost … [a] financial penalty," said Bridgman. "They get engagement on their platform. They get money. Everyone wins except for Canadians, Canadian businesses and Canadian democracy."
Meta did not respond to CBC/Radio-Canada’s request for comment.
How we uncovered the network

Using a combination of corporate documents, on-the-ground reporting in Vietnam, and software including DomainTools, Darkside and OSINT Industries, the CBC/Radio-Canada team was able to expose how this network of Facebook pages and websites, which targeted audiences in the U.K., Europe, United States and Canada, is connected to HTV Network.
It started with a June 2026 report by the Media Ecosystem Observatory investigating "Facebook's News Slop Economy," which identified hundreds of Facebook pages and websites managed out of Vietnam.
CBC/Radio-Canada built off that report, discovering a unique email address — containing "kolax9843" — on one of the websites MEO identified.

That email was the primary contact email for dozens of low-quality, cookie-cutter sites, including one called Autulu. Ad-laden articles from that URL in particular were shared by more than 20 Facebook pages, including "Man City Daily News" or "Wonderful World News," with more than 50,000 followers combined.

One verified Facebook page, "Danny Fernandes," named after the Canadian musician, has more than a million followers and has shared posts that included phrases like "how eight million Democrat votes just vanished" or "Kamala stepdaughter suddenly posted a bold message on Trump Inauguration day."
Fernandes did not respond to CBC.
"The deeper you dig, the more depressing it gets," said Bridgman. "At this scale of followers and number of accounts, this is likely a well-performing business."
CBC/Radio-Canada discovered another website featuring the "kolax9843" email: the company site for FG Media Corp., which contained a photo showing a group of people standing in front of a sign.
The company: HTV Network

Images posted by HTV employees identified by CBC/Radio-Canada on Facebook and TikTok show a busy office, and the company frequently posted ads on Facebook for content marketing jobs paying up to more than double the average yearly salary in Vietnam.

One HTV Network employee, on their personal Facebook page, even posted a photo of them at work. On a computer in the background of the photo, a web browser shows the employee is logged in as a manager for a Facebook page called "I Love Rugby - Kelce." The hyperlinks on that Facebook page took users to the Autulu website.
The "kolax9843" email was also present on a website called Longbientruck, which was registered to Ngo Anh Tan. Domain info showed a phone number that matched the HTV Network website.
Corporate records showed HTV Network Company Limited was created in 2024, with 7 billion Vietnamese dong (or about $350,000 Cdn) in seed money. The corporate records include the same phone number.
The CEO in those records: Ngo Anh Tan.
After CBC/Radio-Canada reached out, HTV added a disclaimer that declares the articles are "fictional and intended solely for entertainment purposes."
Low-quality AI content
The advent of AI has led to an industry of creators who produce cheap, low-quality content at scale.

This, combined with changes to the monetization policies at Meta in 2025, has led to a proliferation of this type of content, said Craig Silverman, co-founder of the Indicator, a publication dedicated to exposing digital deception.
"This kind of AI-generated slop is very clearly not a priority for the company," said Silverman.

"For years, Meta was really focused on rolling out a variety of technical measures and human oversight to eradicate exactly this type of content. Now Meta, through its own action, has just decided to throw in the towel on it. To me, it’s just completely astounding."
Meta did not respond to queries about whether these pages violated their Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior policy.
In Vietnam, Facebook serves roughly 60 to 70 million people, generating $1 billion US in annual revenue for the company in 2018.

"What's interesting with Vietnam [is] you have a very sizable youth population that's highly entrepreneurial and well-educated," said Victoire Rio, executive director of What To Fix, a non-profit that focuses on policy changes and accountability for Big Tech.
"A lot of the actors … are operating very openly without any form of obvious accountability."
