articles.title: Habagat, trough of TD to drench Luzon, Visayas Wednesday
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon or habagat and the trough of a tropical depression outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) will bring rains over Luzon and parts of the Visayas…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The southwest monsoon or habagat and the trough of a tropical depression outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) will bring rains over Luzon and parts of the Visayas on Wednesday, the state weather bureau said.

According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), occasional rains will persist over Zambales, Bataan, Tarlac, Pampanga, Cavite, Batangas, and Occidental Mindoro.
Because of the habagat, cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms are also expected in Metro Manila, the rest of Luzon, Aklan, and Antique.
Moreover, the Ilocos Region, Cordillera Administrative Region, Cagayan Valley and Aurora may experience cloudy skies with scattered rains due to the trough of the tropical depression.
“Ito ‘yung dati nating binantayan na si Pilandok na may international name na Krovan,” weather specialist Chenel Dominguez said in Pagasa’s morning weather briefing.
(This is the same system we previously monitored as Pilandok, with the international name Krovan.)
“Umaabot ‘yung extension ng kaulapan neto dito sa may Northern Luzon na ito rin ang nagdadala ng mga pag-ulan dito sa lugar na ito,” she added.
(Its cloudiness extends over Northern Luzon, which is also bringing rains to the area.)
Meanwhile, in Mindanao and the rest of Visayas, hot and humid weather is likely to persist.
No low-pressure area (LPA) is being monitored by Pagasa within PAR this Wednesday. However, the formation of an LPA is not being ruled out by the bureau.
“By Friday, September 11, inaasahan natin, may posibilidad tayong mabuo na low pressure area na magpapalakas dito sa ating habagat,” Dominguez said.
(By Friday, September 11, we expect that a low-pressure area may form, which could strengthen the habagat.) /jpv

articles.title: Singapore boosts PM’s salary by $1m amid major pay rise for ministers
articles.summary:
The affluent city-state has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance

Singapore’s prime minister has been given a $1m pay…

blocks.text: Singapore’s prime minister has been given a $1m pay rise as the affluent city-state announced a dramatic one-off salary boost for government ministers.
The pay increases add more than 60% to what are already the world’s highest ministerial salaries.

Singapore has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance. The issue is nevertheless politically sensitive, with cabinet members’ income far exceeding that of most ordinary citizens.
Prime minister Lawrence Wong’s benchmark annual salary will rise from S$2.2m ($1.7m) to S$3.6m ($2.8m).
The deputy prime minister’s benchmark will lift from S$1.8m to S$3m. Cabinet ministers will get between S$1.8m and S$2.8m, depending on the seniority and weight of their portfolio.
Wong said he would donate the entire increase of his salary to “suitable good causes” during his term.

Even before the raise, the Singaporean prime minister’s paycheck vastly outstripped the wages of many other leaders, including in the US and other G7 nations. The US president earns $400,000 a year, while the UK prime minister is paid about $230,000 annually.

“Political salaries are a difficult and emotive issue,” said Wong, whose long-ruling People’s Action Party dominates Singapore’s parliament and its 21-member cabinet. “The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely, and why many feel strongly about the matter.”
However, the issue is “ultimately about whether Singapore will continue to have the quality of political leadership we need to take our country forward” in the decades ahead, he said.
“Our starting point is this: good government depends on good leadership.”
The South-east Asian nation, which last adjusted ministerial salaries 15 years ago, is regularly ranked among the world’s least corrupt countries.
Wong said the pay raises were recommended by an independent committee, adding that existing office holders would not be moved immediately to the new benchmarks.
They will receive a one-off adjustment of up to 9% from 15 October, depending on individual circumstances, including performance.

articles.title: 'Cheapest' in the world? Immigration cites foreign fees in defending P240 border charge
articles.summary: Immigration says its proposed P240 border fee is cheapest. Are the foreign charges comparable?

blocks.text: September 9, 2026 | 7:58am
MANILA, Philippines — The Bureau of Immigration defended its proposed P240 border security fee as the "cheapest" compared with charges abroad

Immigration Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado claimed that countries worldwide have adopted modern border security systems similar to the proposed Civil Aviation and Immigration Security Services (CAISS), with passengers also charged for the service.

Viado cited the foreign charges during an August 24 House hearing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Justice and its attached agencies after Caloocan 2nd District Rep. Egay Erice (Caloocan) questioned the additional cost to travelers.
"Ito pong sistema po na ito, ginagamit na po 'yan worldwide. Hindi lang po natin siguro napapansin pero ang ibang bansa po nilalagay po 'yan na kasama ng gastusin sa mga ticket," Viado said.
("This system is being used worldwide. Perhaps we just do not notice it, but other countries include these charges in the cost of airline tickets.")

CAISS is a proposed P10.74-billion public-private partnership with US-based Securiport LLC that would modernize the BI's border management system through biometrics, passenger information processing, identity screening and risk assessment.
Under the proposal, the private partner would finance the system and recover its investment through user fees charged to travelers entering and departing the Philippines.
The proposed charge is $4, or around P240, each time an international traveler enters or leaves the country, or about P480 for a round trip.
How foreign charges compare
Vlado said Australia charges around P2,600 per passenger, Singapore P2,400, Japan P1,200, Hong Kong P1,500 and Thailand P1,800.
All are higher than the proposed P240 charge, but they are not all fees for the same type of border security service.
The examples he cited range from airport security fees to passenger service charges and departure taxes that are not directly equivalent to the Philippine proposal.
Australia imposes a AUD70 (about P3,157) Passenger Movement Charge on people departing the country, which is collected with the airline ticket.

Singapore's Changi Airport charges departing passengers a S$46.40 (about P2,902) Passenger Service and Security Fee. The charge goes to airport operations, maintenance and infrastructure, rather than immigration processing alone.

Japan, meanwhile, imposes a 3,000-yen (about P1,222) International Tourist Tax on most departing travelers. The tax is separate from airport security charges. At Narita International Airport, for instance, departing international passengers pay a separate 700-yen Passenger Security Service Charge.

Hong Kong International Airport has a HK$65 (about P518) Passenger Security Charge specifically used for airport security facilities and systems. Separately, Hong Kong imposes a HK$200 (about P1,595) Air Passenger Departure Tax.

Thailand's six major Airports of Thailand-operated airports charge international departing passengers 1,120 baht (P2,129) under a Passenger Service Charge that supports airport safety, operations, infrastructure and services.
Erice had questioned Viado's Hong Kong comparison, saying he had not noticed such a charge during his trips there.
"You said Hong Kong is doing this. I've been traveling to Hong Kong for quite some time pero wala akong nakikitang ganon," Erice said.
Viado said such charges may not be obvious because they are incorporated into airline ticket prices.
'Not a tax'

Viado also rejected concerns that the proposed charge would run counter to government efforts to reduce travel costs for overseas Filipino workers, arguing that CAISS would impose a service fee rather than a tax.

"Ito po kasi ay hindi po ito form ng tax. Ito po ay service fee," Viado said. "Hindi po namin pwedeng ipasa sa madlang bayan, taong bayan, sa ordinary taxpayer po ang paggastos po dito. Ang gagastos po dito ay ang mga taong nagta-travel."
("This is not a form of tax. This is a service fee. We cannot pass the cost on to the general public or ordinary taxpayers. The people who travel will bear the cost.")
Viado said employers of OFWs would shoulder the charge as part of travel expenses they are required to cover.

"Ang employers po, under an executive order and under various agreements with other countries, ang sumasagot po niyan ng gastusin po sa pamasahe... Kung sakaling ma-approve-an po ito, 'yung service fee po na ito ay sasagutin ng companies that intend to employ our OFWs," Viado said.

("Employers, under an executive order and various agreements with other countries, shoulder airfare expenses... Should this be approved, the service fee will be shouldered by companies that intend to employ our OFWs.")
Existing overseas employment rules require principals or employers of agency-hired land-based workers to shoulder round-trip airfare, among other recruitment and placement costs.
The CAISS project and its proposed passenger fee remain under government review.

articles.title: US slaps import ban on Canadian alcohol and other goods
articles.summary: It is the latest escalation in a trade war between the two countries, and comes as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on US goods come into force.

blocks.text: The US is banning Canadian products, including alcohol, dairy, and motor vehicles, as Canadian retaliatory tariffs on American goods come into force.

In a series of executive orders on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump wrote that "Canada is discriminating in fact against the commerce of the United States," and ordered the ban, which comes into effect on 29 September.
Earlier on Tuesday, Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a video address that Canada's pivot away from the US as its largest trading partner "will come at a cost".
Both US and Canadian officials have said they would like to strike a deal, but no new talks have been scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August.

articles.title: Police maintain perimeter security as Romualdez remains hospitalized
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Police personnel continue to provide perimeter security outside Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City amid the ongoing confinement of former House Speaker Martin…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Police personnel continue to provide perimeter security outside Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City amid the ongoing confinement of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez, who is reportedly being treated for various ailments.
Romualdez, who was arrested Monday over a P7.4-billion plunder case, is currently under the custody of the Philippine National Police (PNP) while confined at the medical center.

Police deployed outside the medical center as of 6 a.m. on Wednesday told the INQUIRER that they are on a shifting schedule to maintain 24/7 security while the former House speaker remains at the hospital.
Another unit of PNP personnel was deployed inside the medical center’s lobby.
On Tuesday, San Juan police chief Col. Anthony Gantang conducted an inspection of their deployment in and around the hospital.
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla earlier said they will request the Sandiganbayan to transfer Romualdez to the PNP General Hospital at Camp Crame in Quezon City.
Remulla announced this as he said that the former speaker had suffered a stroke and a transient ischemic attack—or the temporary blockage of blood to part of the brain—last July.

On Monday, the Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez, former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co, and two others, hours after the Office of the Ombudsman filed the nonbailable plunder case.
The charges stemmed from allegations that they received around P7.4 billion in kickbacks from government projects between 2022 and 2025.
The former House speaker was arrested at the medical center hours after the arrest warrant issuance on Monday, while his three co-accused remain at large. /jpv

articles.title: Brahminy kite rescued in Tayabas City
articles.summary: LUCENA CITY — A Brahminy kite (Haliastur indus), locally known as “lawin,” was found at a business establishment in Tayabas City, Quezon, on Monday (Sept. 7). The City Environment and Natural…

blocks.text: LUCENA CITY — A Brahminy kite (Haliastur indus), locally known as “lawin,” was found at a business establishment in Tayabas City, Quezon, on Monday (Sept. 7).

The City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) said in a report that the medium-sized bird of prey was immediately turned over to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources for proper care and disposition.

The Brahminy kite is a raptor commonly found in coastal and lowland areas. As both a predator and scavenger, it plays an important role in maintaining ecological balance by feeding on small animals and carrion, according to wildlife literature.
CENRO reminded the public that hunting, collecting, or possessing wildlife is prohibited and punishable under Republic Act No. 9147, or the Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act of 2001.
“Report any form of abuse or illegal activity that may harm our environment and natural resources,” the office said. /jpv

articles.title: Heavy rain to hit already soaked Luzon areas Wednesday
articles.summary: Habagat and a tropical cyclone's trough may bring heavy rain across parts of Luzon.

blocks.text: September 9, 2026 | 7:30am
PAGASA's 24-hour rainfall forecast for Sept. 9, 2026 shows 50 to 100 mm of rain over parts of Luzon.
PAGASA

MANILA, Philippines — More heavy rain is forecast across parts of Luzon on Wednesday, September 9, with PAGASA warning that already saturated areas may face greater risks from flooding and landslides after days of rainfall.

In its 5 a.m. weather advisory, PAGASA said the southwest monsoon could bring 50 to 100 millimeters of rain over Tarlac, Zambales, Bataan, Pampanga, Pangasinan, Cavite, Batangas and Occidental Mindoro.
Another 50 to 100 mm is forecast over Ilocos Sur, La Union, Benguet, Quirino, Isabela and Aurora due to the trough of tropical cyclone Krovanh.
"Forecast rainfall may be higher in mountainous and elevated areas. Moreover, impacts in some areas may be worsened by significant antecedent rainfall," PAGASA said.
The weather bureau advised disaster officials in affected areas to take measures to protect lives and property.
Heavy rain is also forecast to continue Thursday, while the rainfall outlook broadens considerably by Friday.
Occidental Mindoro may receive 100 to 200 mm on Friday, while 50 to 100 mm is forecast over a wide swath of Luzon, including Metro Manila, as well as parts of Bicol and Western Visayas.

articles.title: Meta continues to run ads promoting child sexual abuse material in India - report
articles.summary: The report follows a BBC Eye investigation that found Instagram running paid ads promoting such material in India.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains descriptions of abuse
Meta ran hundreds of paid ads with artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse imagery, including several in India, over the past 10 months, a new report by US-based campaigners has found.

The report comes two months after the Indian government ordered Meta to remove all ads and content promoting child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on Instagram. This was in the aftermath of a BBC Eye investigation which found that Instagram was running paid adverts promoting CSAM in India.
Washington-based Tech Transparency Project (TTP), external says it found 332 adverts with CSAM that ran on Facebook and Instagram, the majority of them (274) in August this year.

When the BBC wrote to Meta about these findings, they said in a statement, "We don't tolerate nudify apps or any kind of child exploitation, whether real or AI-generated. These criminals constantly shift tactics to evade detection, which is why we keep strengthening our detection and enforcement."

The TTP report, published on Tuesday, says that it identified several photos of real children, including a member of a European royal family, that were used in the ads and then manipulated using AI. It says more than a dozen ads appeared on Meta platforms even after TTP made the company aware of its findings.
About a quarter (84) of the ads ran in India and 78 of these were published after the Indian government's order on removing CSAM and its meeting with senior Meta officials.
After the BBC investigation, several Indian agencies including the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights and the National Human Rights Commission have said they are examining the matter.
The distribution of CSAM is a criminal offence in India, while Meta's policy states that ads must not contain content that sexually exploits or endangers children.

When the BBC contacted Meta about its investigation, it said that when it becomes aware of apparent child exploitation, it reports it to the US-based National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in compliance with its legal obligations.
The NCMEC is the centralised global reporting system for the online sexual exploitation of children.
But Bhuwan Ribhu, the founder of Just Rights for Children, a network of more than 250 organisations working to prevent violence against children in India, says this is not enough.

Just Rights for Children has filed a petition in India's Supreme Court, citing the BBC's findings, and asked for directions to social media platforms for mandatory reporting and identification of those promoting child sexual abuse material
"Social media companies are clearly flouting Indian laws by not reporting child sexual abuse content to Indian law enforcement agencies as mandated by our child protection laws," said Ribhu.

The TTP, a research initiative of the non-profit Campaign for Accountability that seeks to hold large technology companies accountable, said it found 332 ads featuring CSAM on Instagram and Facebook running in the US, UK, EU, Australia and India. They say they have reported all the ads to NCMEC.
According to TTP, almost all the ads they found start with a photo of a child, and, as the video plays, the photo is manipulated by AI to show them engaging in a graphic sexual act.

TTP described one ad which ran in India as: A photo of a preteen girl animated so that she performs a graphic sex act, with a voiceover that says, "There are no restrictions. All the characters are real people and there are many options. This is the AI men actually use." The BBC has not seen this ad.
According to TTP, the ad was posted by more than 50 different handles in India over a fortnight in August this year.
In July, after BBC's investigation, Meta had put out a detailed post on its website, external about how it fights child exploitation on its apps.
"Anyone on our platforms can report ads if they believe they violate our policies," it said.

TTP said that it tried reporting ads via Meta's own reporting system and that of the 84 ads that ran in India, they were able to report 55. Meta only gives the option of reporting ads when they are live.
For 43 of these, TTP got a reply that said, "We've taken a look and found that this ad doesn't go against our Advertising Standards."
For 11 ads, they were told that the content had already been removed. They haven't received a response yet for one ad.

When the BBC reached out to Meta for a comment, they said, "we've built strong defenses, including systems that block violating ads as well as ongoing monitoring in case we initially miss something: that's why many of the ads flagged to us had already been removed, most had fewer than 200 impressions, and the total ad spend was under $5,000".
TTP said that when it reached out to Meta for a response, all the ads they reported were removed.

This was similar to what happened during the BBC's investigation. When the BBC used Meta's reporting system to report one of the ads featuring child sexual abuse to Instagram, the platform did not take it down.

Later, when the BBC asked Meta for comment, it said it had already disabled several adverts and suspended the accounts posting them. The company said it had removed additional ads, disabled more accounts and blocked URLs for other content that violated its policies in response to the BBC's findings.
TTP said that the vast majority of the 332 ads they found directed users to AI image or video generation apps, mostly from Chinese developers.
The report alleged that by advertising these apps using images of child sexual abuse, the implication is that they can be used for creating or viewing CSAM.
Meta has said it prohibits, external promotion of nudify apps, which use AI to create fake non-consensual nude or sexually explicit images.

One of India's top cyber police officers, Shikha Goel, who is director of the Cyber Security Bureau in the Indian state of Telangana, told the BBC that one of the biggest challenges with CSAM is "the ease with which users can move from one platform to another, making it harder to nab them".
"We are hopeful that the government will be addressing this in its latest interactions with social media intermediaries and direct them accordingly," she added.
The ads that BBC had found in its investigation also directed users to another app - the messaging app Telegram - where they could buy the material for as little as 99 rupees [$1.05; £0.80].
Telegram told the BBC at the time that the company uses both automated and human moderation to tackle CSAM, and that it has "virtually eliminated the public spread of CSAM" on its platform.

Ads on Meta's platforms are only published after first being approved by its moderation technology. Its review system relies primarily on automation and is designed to check images, video, text and audio, as well as who the ad is targeting and where links send them to.
After the BBC's investigation, Meta had said that "no system is perfect" and that "determined criminals continue to try to exploit our platform, including through our advertising systems".
But TTP found that several of the ads featuring child sexual abuse were placed by Meta's own ad agency partners in China.
These partners, known as "resellers", channel billions of dollars' worth of Chinese advertising onto Facebook and Instagram. The partners did not respond to TTP's questions.
TTP said that new ads have continued to appear even after they made Meta aware of their report's findings. They shared details of 17 ads including 11 that ran in India on 1-2 September.

articles.title: Hegseth is shaking up the Pentagon as the US wages war - but at what cost?
articles.summary: The upheaval in the military could shape the legacy of Trump's second term, writes the BBC's Tom Bateman.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
ByTom Bateman
State department correspondent, Washington
The United States military is at the centre of a fight on two fronts.

First is President Donald Trump's attempt to prise the Strait of Hormuz from Iran's grip; the latest phase of his stalemated war in the Gulf which is drawing in US forces and equipment from around the globe.

The second is a culture war at home in which Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is conducting a promised shake-up at the Pentagon, sparking bitter recriminations and a string of departures including the top civilian in charge of the US Army last week.

The upheaval has triggered questions that could shape the legacy of Trump's second term. Is the US military being stretched to a point that could risk global security? And are these shifts leaving America's extraordinary global network of alliances vulnerable?
Last Monday there was dramatic news from the Pentagon.
One of its most senior political leaders, Dan Driscoll, stepped down as US Secretary of the Army.

Driscoll is not exactly a household name in America, let alone outside it. But his departure mattered. It was the latest twist in a power struggle within the fortress-like walls of the Pentagon over the future of the world's most formidable fighting force.
Driscoll had clashed repeatedly with Hegseth over the nature and speed of military reform. His departure was the latest in a long line of top leaders removed or sidelined by Hegseth.

The level of concern became clear as one Republican Senator Thom Tillis - a frequent Trump critic - called for Hegseth to be fired. "I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," he said.

"This is not good news. You know, for our nation, for the army," H.R. McMaster, who served as Trump's National Security Adviser during his first term, told CBS when asked about Driscoll's departure. "Secretary Driscoll was pushing… a modernisation agenda to catch the army up."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Driscoll, seen here meeting Ukraine's Zelensky in November, resigned last week

blocks.text: Image source, Ukrainian Presidential Press Office
Driscoll, seen here meeting Ukraine's Zelensky in November, resigned last week

The backstory of Driscoll's resignation cut deep into issues about the readiness of the US Army. Driscoll wanted urgent modernisation by adding drones throughout ordinary army formations to make it adept for 21st Century warfare.

He said the Ukraine war had shown how the battlefield had changed, with cheap drones and anti-missile systems challenging the US military with its vast bureaucracy and expensive procurement processes.
Hegseth had in fact initiated much of this modernisation plan but subsequently came into conflict with Driscoll, according to reports, as well as with others advocating its rapid expansion.

A source familiar with last week's departure said Driscoll had raised concerns within the administration about army readiness and transformation, which Driscoll said Hegseth was "blocking" specifically by firing the generals responsible.
Jon Duffy, a retired Navy captain and former White House defence policy official, said Driscoll's resignation showed how far Hegseth had "hollowed out" the military leadership at a critical moment.
"You lose the [army] secretary, the chief of staff and other senior leaders driving modernisation, it creates a lot of uncertainty and it disrupts momentum," he said.

"That uncertainty at leadership levels has downstream effects on the force," added Duffy, who had a 30-year career and commanded US warships before joining the White House during the second Obama administration.
Hegseth to US top brass: "We became the woke department. But not anymore"
In public, Hegseth - a former Army National Guardsman and Fox News pundit - has spent much of his time calling for cultural change to the US military.

He has vowed to end what he called "woke" initiatives and scrap "stupid" rules of engagement he said constrained war fighters' "lethality". He tore up diversity programmes, banned beards and railed against seeing "fat generals in the halls of the Pentagon".

He removed or sidelined the top uniformed officers in charge of the Army, Navy and Air Force as well as at least two dozen generals, admirals and civilian defence leaders, including some of the US military's most decorated officers, often with little explanation.

One critic compares the changes in the top ranks to President Xi Jinping's political purges of the Chinese military which are said to have left serious deficiencies in command structure and readiness.

"We've been conducting a military purge as well, and that has real effects on the ability of our military to be able to discharge its responsibilities," Michael Schiffer, a former top Pentagon official who covered East Asia from 2009 to 2012 under the Obama presidency, told the BBC.

"The way in which [Hegseth is] shaking them up… is bringing on board an awful lot of risk without any apparent way to be able to address or ameliorate it," said Schiffer, who is now a senior fellow at the liberal think-tank the Center for American Progress.

Asked last week about Driscoll's departure, Vice-President JD Vance defended Hegseth, saying he was in "strident agreement" about the need for a culture shift after what he called 40 years of lost wars and "military misadventures".
"What Pete came in wanting to do was revive the warrior spirit in the United States of America," Vance said.

In a statement, the White House told the BBC that President Trump had "full confidence in Secretary Hegseth and the entire Department of War whose record of success in Operation Epic Fury, Operation Absolute Resolve, and Operation Midnight Hammer speaks for itself".
Trump has continued to back Hegseth, standing by him during controversies such as Signalgate and describing him in a phone interview with NBC News last month as "actually one of my best".
Ezra Cohen, a former Under Secretary of Defence during the first Trump administration, described Hegseth's reforms as "bringing in fresh thinking and a more forward-leaning attitude".
But the reported friction among the military leadership and the stalemate with Iran has raised questions about the future of the US military at a critical moment.
'Vulnerabilities in Europe'

Trump's order to launch strikes on Iran on 28 February led to a significant global redistribution of US military resources over the subsequent months. US weapons stored in Europe and Asia were transferred from those regions to replenish supplies in the Gulf.
Europe is now feeling significant "blowback", according to Professor Liana Fix, a Germany-based expert at the Council on Foreign Relations.

She said the lack of communication by the Trump administration with its Nato and European allies ahead of the attack on Iran left relations reeling and accelerated a strategic decision already in process to shift some US military resources away from Europe, particularly as Trump complained that his European allies weren't helping.

Prof Fix said in that context Russian President Vladimir Putin had escalated so-called "hybrid" attacks involving armed drones or sabotage attacks on Nato countries like Germany. Russia denies carrying out the attacks.

"What [Putin] is seeing is not a united stance from the United States and the Europeans to further increase pressure on Russia… he sees that they are weakening, that there are windows and openings of vulnerabilities in Europe," she told the BBC.

Last month, CIA Director John Ratcliffe paid a highly unusual visit to Moscow. He is reported to have delivered a warning to the Kremlin not to test Nato's resolve. But at the same time, one of Hegseth's top officials at the Pentagon, Elbridge Colby, was in Europe to push countries to spend more on their own defence.

Washington had announced a cut of 5,000 from a total 40,000 US troops based in Germany, while a Biden-era plan to deploy a US battalion with long-range Tomahawk missiles to the country was being dropped.

The drawdowns in Europe fit the Trump administration's strategy that predates the Iran war. It sees the Pacific region and Washington's rivalry with China as America's number one national security challenge.
Watch: Hegseth hits back after a Democratic senator calls him a "failure" over Iran war

But while the fallout from the Iran war has exacerbated Trump's irritation with Europe and accelerated some US military moves away from the region, it has not been to the immediate benefit of the US presence in the Pacific.
In fact, Washington has also pulled resources from there. Carrier forces were diverted from the Pacific to the Gulf, including the USS Abraham Lincoln and later the Japan-based USS George Washington.

The war is widely assessed to have left critical stocks of American ammunition badly depleted. The US fired about a third of its 3,000-strong stockpile of Tomahawk attack missiles, according to the Washington DC-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

Its air defence munitions were burned up at an even higher rate, with nearly 1,500 Patriot interceptors - used to shoot down aircraft and cruise and ballistic missiles - fired out of a stockpile of around 2,300, according to the CSIS.
White House Principle Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said America's "military might" was "stronger than it's ever been".
"The United States Military has more than enough munitions, ammo, and stockpiles to serve all of the Commander-in-Chief's strategic goals and beyond," she said.
Meanwhile Ezra Cohen, the former Trump defence official who is now a fellow at the Hudson Institute, described the president as having degraded Iran's conventional military threat.

Iran's proxy groups are weaker than ever, he said, and in many places they have been completely obliterated, meaning "the president now has additional options and forces in the region to strike other Iranian targets, including nuclear targets, at will".

The strikes might yet take place again. Thousands of troops, including the 82nd Airborne Division, were sent to the Middle East more than six months ago for a deployment that is now stretching into 2027 with no obvious end in sight.

Pictures last week of the USS Abraham Lincoln docking in Thailand with a rusting hull after a gruelling nine months at sea in the Gulf were pounced on by Iran. The regime tried to portray it as a symbol of America's spent efforts.

Hegseth, meanwhile, forcefully rejected claims of abysmal conditions on board. But the narrative war reflected the challenge for Trump and Hegseth as they fight to transform the Pentagon while waging a costly, protracted war.

articles.title: 'Constantly on my mind' - 9/11 agony goes on for bereaved, 25 years on
articles.summary: As the 25th anniversary approaches, the wait for the alleged mastermind of the attack to be put on trial goes on.

blocks.text: Image source, Tom Resta
John Resta and his wife Sylvia
The US government has described it as the "most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history".
But a quarter of a century on, the trial of its alleged mastermind is yet to begin and families of those killed fear that time for justice to be delivered is running out.

Tom Resta's brother John and his wife Sylvia, who was seven months pregnant, were among the almost 3,000 people killed on 11 September 2001 when hijackers flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon in Virginia. Another crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after the passengers fought back.

The couple had been preparing their unborn baby's nursery, painting it with characters from the children's television show Blue's Clues in the days before 9/11. They had dreamed of having a baby and doted on the children of friends and family.
On the day of the attacks, the couple - both traders - were working on the 92nd floor of the north tower of the World Trade Center.
"After all this time, it still chokes me up," Resta told the BBC through tears. While 25 years have passed, he said 9/11 was "almost constantly" on his mind.

Resta has been to the US naval base of Guantanamo Bay four times to watch complex pre-trial proceedings for alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and his co-defendants - a process he describes as "laborious and tedious".

A military prison was established on the base in south-eastern Cuba during the "war on terror" that followed the 9/11 attacks, and Mohammed - often referred to as KSM - has now been held there for 20 years without ever being convicted.
Relatives of victims enter a lottery process to attend the proceedings in a high-security courtroom, where thick glass separates them and members of the press from the defendants.
The pre-trial process has been going on for so long that it has now been presided over by five different military judges.
Last month, as the 25th anniversary approached, there was a flurry of movement and something of a breakthrough, with a trial date set for Mohammed for June 2028.
But Resta said he was bracing himself for further delays, and with so much time having passed, some of his relatives feared they would not live long enough to see the trial.

"My father will be 98 in November, and I don't think he's expecting to see it. I have a lot of family members - aunts, uncles - that would all like to see it happen. But my parents in particular, I don't think they expect to live long enough," he said.
"Hopefully all the defendants will still be alive by the time we get to trial. That's a big worry," he added.

blocks.caption: Image caption, A tribute in light above the New York City skyline, at the 2024 anniversary

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
A tribute in light above the New York City skyline, at the 2024 anniversary
Resta's concerns that a trial could still be further delayed were shared by relatives of other 9/11 victims.

Earlier this year, Stephan Gerhardt made his sixth trip to Guantanamo. He said seeing convictions for the death of his younger brother Ralph was vital for him, but something he wished he no longer had to think about.

"I want to concentrate on the memories," he said. "I still have Ralph's car. I'm trying to restore it and get it in pristine shape again… We were recently visiting my parents, and we found some of his things that they were holding onto, and the emotion behind it is like, 'yeah, this is just some old stuff, but it belonged to my little brother'."
Gerhardt said his "biggest concern" was that he wanted to see Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators convicted before they died.

"They're getting elderly… I don't want them to pass away without being convicted, because that would be an injustice to all the family members - that we captured these people, but we never got to try them and convict them for the mass murder that they did of our loved ones."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed as he appeared on the FBI's Most Wanted website

blocks.text: Image source, FBI
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed as he appeared on the FBI's Most Wanted website

Mohammed has been charged with offences including conspiracy and murder, with 2,976 victims listed on the charge sheet. He is accused of conceiving the idea of training pilots to fly commercial planes into buildings and taking those plans to Osama bin Laden, leader of the militant Islamist group al-Qaeda.
He has previously said he planned the "9/11 operation from A to Z".

But days after the trial date was set for 2028, the military judge threw out confessions made by Mohammed to FBI agents on Guantanamo Bay after he was brought there from secret CIA prisons known as "black sites", which he had been held in for years. In his ruling, the judge described Mohammed's treatment by the CIA as "extraordinary physical and mental abuse".
He said the confessions were not voluntary and could not be used against Mohammed at trial.
Experts say the torture of Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators has been the main reason for the lengthy delays in the case.
"Every single issue has been litigated through the issue of torture," said Kasey McCall-Smith, an international law professor at Edinburgh University.
She said the defendants were subjected to "years of abuse", including waterboarding and stress positions.

blocks.caption: Image caption, John and Sylvia Resta on their wedding day

blocks.text: John and Sylvia Resta on their wedding day

John Ryan, author of America's Trial: Torture and the 9/11 Case on Guantanamo Bay, said last month's ruling means prosecutors lose what they had described as their best evidence against Mohammed, but it is unclear how much it will impact the case.

The prosecution has other evidence, Ryan says, including intercepted phone calls and secret recordings, but whether they can feature in the trial is not yet guaranteed. "Mohammad's team and the other defence teams will file motions to suppress some of these categories of evidence, as well."

During the George W Bush administration, the US admitted using "enhanced interrogation techniques" to acquire information from suspects but said these methods saved lives and never amounted to torture. President Barack Obama banned them on his second day in office.

blocks.caption: Image caption, President George W Bush on Air Force One after the attacks

blocks.text: President George W Bush on Air Force One after the attacks
Relatives of the victims say the torture of the defendants has so far blocked their right to justice.

"If we would've not tortured them, the legal implications here would've been much, much simpler. They probably would've been sentenced to death a long time ago," said Gerhardt. "I can't control what the government did, and we've got to live with the impacts."

Both Gerhardt and Resta travelled to Guantanamo in early 2025 when Mohammed and two of his co-defendants had been due to plead guilty under a controversial deal struck with US government prosecutors, through which they would not face a death penalty trial.

The BBC was with them at the base when the pleas were paused at the last minute after the US government argued that to "deprive the government and the American people of a public trial as to the respondents' guilt and the possibility of capital punishment" would cause "irreparable" harm.
Legal wrangling over the validity of the deal is continuing.
Some victims' relatives viewed the deal as the only way through, while others criticised it as too lenient and lacking transparency.
Resta said he had supported the deal to secure convictions.

"My philosophy is these guys are not the kind of people that should be out walking the streets, but as far as I'm concerned, they can just stay right where they are. I just want them convicted," he said.
Brett Eagleson, whose dad Bruce was killed in the attacks, said he wanted a full trial, not a plea deal.

"It's not so much that I'm taking an opinion on life or death for these prisoners, but I believe in the judicial system and I believe that the process works and I believe that a trial and discovery and sort of a public airing is the way to flush the truth out," he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Brett Eagleson was 15 when his father Bruce was killed

blocks.text: Image source, Brett Eagleson
Brett Eagleson was 15 when his father Bruce was killed
Eagleson described the situation on Guantanamo as "a mess" and said he had decided not to attend any of the pre-trial proceedings there.
"My overall feeling is a sense of betrayal from the US government and a sense of extreme frustration," he said. "They've botched every single part of this trial."
With 25 years having passed since the attacks, he said that while 9/11 was a constant presence in his own life, to the wider public it was "becoming a historical event".
"I think people just assume that we got Bin Laden, we're out of Iraq, the war in Afghanistan's over, and they just assume that chapter has ended."
When the trial does eventually start, at a military court at Guantanamo, it has been estimated that it will last about a year.
Professor Kasey McCall-Smith said the point of the pre-trial proceedings had been determining "what evidence gets in and what evidence doesn't get in".
"If that is agreed in advance, the trial can be more expeditious," she explained.

As the relatives of the victims prepared for another anniversary marking the death of their loved ones, Gerhardt said he was looking forward to a time that the trial was over and he no longer had to think about or travel to Guantanamo.
"It's a place I don't want to come back to. I want to live my life, enjoy my passions and my memories of Ralph," he said.

articles.title: A 3rd festival-goer dies at Burning Man
articles.summary: Authorities have confirmed the death of a third attendee of the Burning Man festival, days after organizers said two other festival-goers had died during the annual event in the Nevada des

image.caption: A satellite image shows the annual Burning Man festival, held in Nevada's Black Rock desert, on Aug. 31. Three attendees died during the weeklong event, officials and organizers say. (Vantor/Handout/Reuters)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Authorities have confirmed the death of a third attendee of the Burning Man festival, days after organizers said two other festival-goers had died during the annual event in the Nevada des
California man dies en route to hospital, days after 2 other deaths
Authorities have confirmed the death of a third attendee of the Burning Man festival, days after organizers said two other festival-goers had died during the annual event in the Nevada desert.

The Washoe County Regional Medical Examiner's Office said in a statement on Tuesday that Armando Ramirez of Truckee, Calif., died while being taken to a hospital in Reno, Nev., roughly 190 kilometres south of the festival.
The 51-year-old was pronounced dead in the ambulance in the early hours of Friday.
"The cause and manner of death are pending the results of additional testing," the examiner's office said. "There is no concern for foul play."

The festival, which runs annually in the desert for about a week and centres on art installations and self-expression, last week announced two other deaths, which were also confirmed on Tuesday by the Pershing County Sheriff's Office.

Craigh Mann, 60, was found dead on Saturday at about 3 p.m. local time, the festival said in a statement. The sheriff's office, which referred to him as Craig Mann, said that he had been in a trailer he shared with his significant other.

The festival said earlier that another festival-goer, a man in his mid-50s, "experienced a medical emergency" and was pronounced dead after receiving emergency care. The sheriff's office identified him as Sampson Tshombe and said he died at the festival's temporary hospital on Thursday.
Authorities said there was no sign of foul play in Mann or Tshombe's deaths, but that both would undergo an autopsy and a toxicology screening, with results coming in six to eight weeks.

This year marks the 40th anniversary of the festival. It began on Aug. 30. and concluded on Monday. Every year, tens of thousands of people flock to the desert to camp in the wilderness and participate in avant-garde performances, with the event culminating in the burning of a large wooden sculpture shaped like a man.

The festival has been marred by death before. More than a half-dozen other deaths have been reported at the festival since it moved from Baker Beach in San Francisco to the Black Rock desert in 1990, The Associated Press reports.
Jerry Allen, Pershing County sheriff and coroner, said in a Monday statement that the festival averages one death a year, according to NBC News.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: PNP reports P3.4-M haul from La Union drug busts in a week
articles.summary: SAN FERNANDO CITY, La Union – The Ilocos Regional Police’s campaign against illegal drugs led to the confiscation of P3.4 million worth of suspected shabu and marijuana plants, during crime…

blocks.text: SAN FERNANDO CITY, La Union – The Ilocos Regional Police’s campaign against illegal drugs led to the confiscation of P3.4 million worth of suspected shabu and marijuana plants, during crime suppression operations conducted from September 1-7.

A police report showed that it conducted 25 operations during which they arrested 24 suspects in possession of 411.48 grams of suspected shabu, 2,740 fully grown marijuana plants, 1,400 marijuana seedlings, and 30 grams of dried marijuana leaves.
The intensified manhunt operations also secured the arrest of 56 fugitives, including seven most wanted persons (MWPs) and 49 other wanted suspects, the report said.
The police’s 20 operations against illegal gambling also led to the arrest of 20 suspects and the confiscation of bet money amounting to P33,457.00.
The drive against loose firearms likewise accounted for nine weapons, consisting of six surrendered and three deposited firearms.

“Our weekly accomplishments reflect the police’s commitment to responsive and effective law enforcement. We will remain relentless in our operations and steadfast in safeguarding the peace, safety, and security of communities across the Ilocos Region,” said Brig. Gen. Crisaleo Tolentino, Ilocos police director, in a statement.
The Ilocos Region is composed of the provinces of Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union and Pangasinan. /jpv

articles.title: Two held, P3.5-M worth of fuel seized in Marinduque
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Two suspects were arrested and around P3.54 million worth of petroleum products and transport equipment were seized in a joint police operation in Gasan, Marinduque,…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Two suspects were arrested and around P3.54 million worth of petroleum products and transport equipment were seized in a joint police operation in Gasan, Marinduque, on Tuesday (Sept. 8).

The suspects were arrested in Barangay Bachao Ibaba after they were caught distributing and dispensing petroleum products using a tanker allegedly without the required Department of Energy (DOE) authority and permit, according to the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) and the MIMAROPA police.

Seized during the operation were about 19,800 liters of petroleum products valued at P1.734 million, consisting of 12,000 liters of premium gasoline, 6,000 liters of diesel and 1,800 liters of unleaded gasoline.

Police also confiscated a blue-and-white 10-wheeler tank lorry valued at about P1.805 million, a black suction hose, the vehicle’s official receipt and certificate of registration, and a delivery receipt.
The total estimated value of the seized petroleum products and equipment was placed at P3.538 million.

The suspects would.be charged for violating Section 2 (a), in relation to Section 3 (h), of Batas Pambansa Blg. 33, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1865, which penalizes unlawful acts involving petroleum products. /jpv

articles.title: Mindoro missionary, teacher Fr. Edgar Javier dies at 77
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro – Divine Word missionary and scholar Fr. Edgar Javier, SVD, who served the Church for five decades, mostly in Mindoro, had passed away on Tuesday (Sept. 8). He was 77.…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro – Divine Word missionary and scholar Fr. Edgar Javier, SVD, who served the Church for five decades, mostly in Mindoro, had passed away on Tuesday (Sept. 8). He was 77.
Javier died at around 10 a.m., according to the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) News.

The Society of the Divine Word (SVD) did not disclose the cause of his death. “We entrust him to God’s loving embrace and give thanks for his life of service, compassion, and missionary zeal,” the SVD said.
Javier’s missionary journey took him from Mindoro to the Pacific and later to the Philippines’ seminaries and theological institutions, where he helped form priests, religious and missionaries.
For Catholic communities in Mindoro, he is particularly remembered for his early missionary service in Occidental Mindoro and ministry among the Mangyan communities.
Born on May 5, 1949 in Guimba town, Nueva Ecija, Javier entered the Christ the King Mission Seminary in 1968 and was ordained a priest on Sept. 5, 1975.
He began his missionary ministry in Mindoro, serving at St. Augustine Parish and the St. Joseph Parish Mangyan Mission in San Jose town, Occidental Mindoro, from 1976 to 1979.
He later served as chancellor of the Apostolic Vicariate of Calapan, which is now the Diocese of Calapan.
Javier pursued advanced studies in missiology at the Pontifical Gregorian University in Rome, earning a licentiate in 1982 and a doctorate in 1985.
He served as a missionary in Samoa from 1985 to 1995 and Fiji from 1995 to 1999 before returning to the Philippines, where he focused on priestly formation, missiological education and research.

He taught at Christ the King Mission Seminary and headed the Mission Institute in Tagaytay before becoming director of the Divine Word Institute of Mission Studies (DWIMS). He also taught at several theological institutions in the Philippines and served as a visiting professor in Vietnam and Macau.
For his former co-faculty at DWIMS, Fr. Andy Peter Lubi, Javier was more than an academic.
“Fr. Egay Javier is an intimately engaging person and a deeply passionate mentor, one who challenges and brings out the best in his students,” Lubi said.
Fr. Renz Hernandez, one of Javier’s students in missiology, said Javier encouraged him to pursue a master’s degree in the field and volunteered to become his thesis adviser.

“As a professor, his way of teaching is engaging and his missiological ideas are profound yet practical. As an adviser, he’s very encouraging and supportive. He reads, checks, and corrects my paper thoroughly,” Hernandez said.
“I will never forget his writing techniques which he imparted to us—the SJA Method (See, Judge, Act) and the RRR Method (Reality, Reflection, Response),” he added.
Javier had marked his 50th year as a priest in 2025. /jpv

articles.title: Teodoro calls out China’s ‘disrespectful’ note at Seoul forum
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr. on Tuesday described China’s latest assertion, written in a letter regarding the South China Sea arbitration, as “actual coercion,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr. on Tuesday described China’s latest assertion, written in a letter regarding the South China Sea arbitration, as “actual coercion, bullying and aggression”.
His denunciation came after a man handed him, on stage, a piece of paper during a question-and-answer session at the Seoul Defense Dialogue, an annual multilateral security forum.

“China’s position on the South China Sea arbitration is clear, consistent, and firm. They have no position. The arbitration violates fundamental principles of international law,” the letter stated as read aloud by Teodoro.
The defense chief slammed China’s assertion, saying that they only refused to recognize the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos) after losing the arbitral tribunal.
The Unclos 2016 ruling is a landmark award that recognizes the Philippines’ claim over the West Philippine Sea.
Teodoro, moreover, said that the move was a blatant disrespect to the international forum, particularly to the Republic of Korea,.

“It not only disrespects, shows, if this is a Chinese position said to me, it not only disrespects international law, throwing Unclos to the floor and trampling upon it, but it also disrespects the basic decency that should be accorded to our most gracious hosts, the Republic of Korea and the rest of the audience here,” he expressed.
He added that China should observe “basic decency.”
Teodoro said in a video posted on Facebook that the man who delivered the letter to him was a Chinese delegate.
The defense chief earlier spoke at the first plenary session attended by international defense leaders, where he pushed for a collaborative security architecture across Asia. /cb

articles.title: Judges speak out after peer got trolled by Sara Duterte diehards
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — An organization of trial court judges reminded the public that judges should be able to perform their duty without fear, after one of them became the subject of online…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — An organization of trial court judges reminded the public that judges should be able to perform their duty without fear, after one of them became the subject of online harassment for issuing an arrest warrant last week against Vice President Sara Duterte.

The Kapunungan sa mga Pilipinong Hukom (Hukom), a group of first- and second-level trial court judges from various provinces, expressed grave concern over the “unfounded accusations” against Judge Maria Angelica de Ramos of Quezon City Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 98, which will hear the grave threats case against the Vice President.

Since the warrant came out on Sept. 4, social media posts mainly by Duterte’s supporters have shared background information on De Ramos, insinuating bias because she was appointed to the post last year by President Marcos.
Some included her photo, with the caption: “Remember the face!”

Duterte on Saturday posted a bail at P360,000 for the charges arising from her online press briefing in November 2024, where she said she had talked to someone to have President Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former Speaker Martin Romualdez killed if an alleged murder plot against her succeeded.
Before the procedure, the Vice President was heard telling her lawyers that she was fearing for her life and she didn’t trust the court, the police or even her own security personnel.

“While freedom to criticize the courts and judicial decisions is vital in a democracy, vilification of judges undermines judicial independence and public confidence in the rule of law,” Hukom said in a statement on Tuesday.
“Judges must decide cases freely, according to law, without fear or pressure—even when rulings are unpopular,” it stressed.

Hukom reminded netizens that social media is “not a courtroom” and that “digital mobs are not justice,” stressing that government officials, including the Vice President, should “stand equal before the courts.”

In a phone interview, Hukom president Rosario Caise said the harassment of judges, either through cyberbullying or Red-tagging, are not just an attack on the person but also on the judiciary as an institution.
“Whatever is presented before the courts, that’s our only basis for our decision… Attacking the judge is likewise attacking the institution,” she told the Inquirer.
Formed in 2018, Hukom had come to the defense of other judges who were vilified online because of their rulings.

They include Judge Marlo Malagar of Manila RTC over his dismissal of a petition to declare the Communist Party of the Philippines and its armed wing New People’s Army as “terrorists”; and Judge Monique Quisumbing-Ignacio of Muntinlupa RTC for dismissing the case against journalists Lady Ann Salem and labor organizer Rodrigo Esparago. /cb

articles.title: July unemployment leaps to 6 percent; highest in postpandemic era
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The country’s labor market showed fresh signs of strain in July as more fresh graduates struggled to find jobs, pushing unemployment to its highest level since the pandemic era.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The country’s labor market showed fresh signs of strain in July as more fresh graduates struggled to find jobs, pushing unemployment to its highest level since the pandemic era.

According to data by the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) released on Tuesday, the unemployment rate surged to 6 percent in July from 4.9 percent in June. This was equivalent to 3.14 million jobless Filipinos, up from 2.59 million in June.
The latest figure marked the third straight month of increase and was the highest in four years, or since June 2022, when unemployment also stood at 6 percent.
This was also the first time unemployment reached the 6-percent level after staying between 4.7 percent and 5.8 percent since the start of the year.

Month-on-month, the labor force participation rate declined to 63.6 percent from 65.1 percent, translating to a labor force of 52.36 million from 53.25 million. But quarter-on-quarter, it increased from 62.7 percent, or 51.3 million.
Metro Manila had the highest unemployment rate at 8.2 percent.

National Statistician Claire Dennis Mapa said the sudden rise in unemployment was due to new participants estimated at 1.33 million who have joined the labor market but are not yet absorbed into the workforce.
The age group of these entrants was pegged at 15 to 24 years old.
The employment rate declined one percentage point in July from 95 percent in June, with the number of employed Filipinos falling to 49.21 million from 50.55 million.
The number of underemployed Filipinos, meanwhile, rose to 12.9 percent from 12.1 percent. This represented 6.33 million underemployed Filipinos, up from 6.11 million in June.
Quality jobs needed
The Department of Economy, Planning and Development (DepDev) said the spike in unemployment is a challenge.

“More Filipinos are participating in the labor market, which means that we need to intensify efforts to attract investments, especially those that create quality jobs,” DepDev Secretary Arsenio Balisacan said.
“The key is to continuously improve the ease of doing business in the country,” he said.

Economist Leonardo Lanzona of the Ateneo de Manila University said the increase in unemployment is no longer a short-term absorption lag, especially since it had been climbing steadily as the share of degree holders among the jobless rose from 26.9 percent in 2020 to the latest figure of 35.6 percent.

“If this were a short-run absorption lag, it would have been corrected already. We have a structural demographic mismanagement problem which means investment incentives are designed to reward capital size rather than job creation,” Lanzona said.

“The economy keeps attracting capital-intensive investment that can’t absorb a growing young workforce—a design flaw no amount of job-matching or reskilling programs can fix without reforming the incentive criteria themselves,” he added. /cb

articles.title: DILG chief: ‘We won’t allow’ Romualdez to stay at private hospital
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Secretary Jonvic Remulla of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) said the agency would ask the Sandiganbayan to have former Speaker Martin Romualdez…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Secretary Jonvic Remulla of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) said the agency would ask the Sandiganbayan to have former Speaker Martin Romualdez transferred, as a person under arrest, from a private hospital to the police medical facility inside Camp Crame.
Remulla announced the plan as the antigraft court ordered Romualdez to appear on Thursday regarding his motion seeking continued hospital confinement following his arrest for plunder on Monday night.

The Leyte congressman, a cousin of President Marcos, was served an arrest warrant and underwent police booking procedures at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, where he had been admitted for anxiety attacks and what Remulla called a “cardiovascular event” hours before the warrant came out.

A motion to have the lawmaker moved to the Philippine National Police General Hospital at Camp Crame, Quezon City, will be filed on Wednesday “just to show you that we won’t allow him to stay at Cardinal Santos,’’ Remulla said.

“We can monitor his condition at Crame, but it’s up to the discretion of the court if he’ll be allowed to be moved to Crame,” he added. “We will give his doctors visitation and practicing rights so they can go to Camp Crame.”

Romualdez, former Ako Bicol Rep. Elizaldy Co and two others were charged with plunder, a nonbailable offense, before the Sandiganbayan over allegations they received more than P7 billion in kickbacks from government projects between 2022 and 2025.

Based on charges prepared by the Office of the Ombudsman, Romualdez and Co were accused of “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen (15) occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion.

The amount allegedly came from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects that were funded under the General Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2022 to 2025.
The P7.44 billion, according to the case, was “specifically traced and laundered [by] setting up and/or using shell or dummy corporations and conduits.”
Respecting legal process
Aside from Romualdez and Co, also named in the charge sheet were a member of the former Speaker’s staff, Jocelyn Sereño, and a certain Felicito Guevarra, the president of a money changer corporation.
In a statement on Monday, Romualdez’s lawyer and spokesperson Ade Fajardo said his client respects the courts and legal process and will face the charges.

“We recognize the public interest surrounding this case. But ultimately, criminal liability must be determined by the evidence presented in court, under the rules and safeguards of our justice system,” Fajardo said.
He said Romualdez was not asking for special treatment but “asks only for the same due process and fair hearing guaranteed to every Filipino.”
Custody
The Sandiganbayan Third Division, in its order on Tuesday, stressed that the court now has custody of Romualdez.

“If there are concerns regarding the accused’s medical condition, it is only this court that can determine whether such condition affects the implementation of the warrant, the confinement of the accused at a hospital, or his commitment to a jail facility,” the court said.
It also issued a subpoena to Romualdez’s doctors Rody Sy, Rogelio Libarres, Kurt Allen Sibayan and Rosalio Torres, ordering their appearance on Thursday.
According to his motion requesting continued hospital stay, Romualdez is suffering from Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, primary hypothyroidism and other illnesses.
According to Remulla, Romualdez suffered a stroke and a transient ischemic attack, or the temporary blockage of blood to a part of the brain, in July.
“It wasn’t that serious. From what I saw, he had no deficiency, but he suffered a cerebrovascular event,” he said.

Regarding security arrangements, Remulla said “We have two armed guards stationed outside his room 24/7. We also have armed guards in the lobby, and a mobile patrol unit waiting outside the hospital.”
Remulla described Romualdez as a “flight risk,” noting that he has “two private jets… three helicopters … and three yachts.”
The DILG on Tuesday also released Romualdez’s official mug shot taken during the booking procedure.
The photo, flashed on screen during a press briefing in Camp Crame, shows Romualdez in a hospital bed with an orange PNP detainee shirt placed on top of his medical gown.
No instruction
The PNP earlier explained that Romualdez could not be made to stand up for the photo or wear the orange shirt due to the medical implements attached to his body.
Remulla maintained he had not received any instruction from President Marcos on how to treat the former House leader.

“The President has no male sibling, so Romualdez is his closest cousin. If you think this was easy for him, it wasn’t,” Remulla said. “If you’re asking whether there were instructions on how to treat him, there was none. Zero.”
Remulla also told reporters that he and Romualdez briefly spoke during the serving of the warrant, noting that they were fraternity brothers at the University of the Philippines.

“He had no requests… I told him, ‘Brother, I hope you understand why I am doing this. It’s nothing personal.’ And he said, ‘It’s okay, I understand.’ That was the entire length of our conversation,” he said.

Reacting to criticism over Romualdez happening to be at a hospital just hours before the warrant was released, the interior secretary said: “That’s the hard part. We do not have the right to intercept (an accused) before the warrant of arrest is issued by the court.”

“They (the accused and his lawyers) knew the charges were filed. They knew the case was raffled, so they got ahead of it. In this case, actually, it’s only with Speaker Martin that that’s happened … I don’t believe in coincidences, so we take it at that,” he said. /cb

articles.title: PH improves rank in int’l education assessment
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Three years after ranking near the bottom of international learning assessments in 2022, the Philippines expanded its reach in 2025, surpassing 18 education systems in reading,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Three years after ranking near the bottom of international learning assessments in 2022, the Philippines expanded its reach in 2025, surpassing 18 education systems in reading, 16 in mathematics, and 14 in science.
Based on the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) results, the Philippines, when ranked from the bottom, placed 15th in science, 17th in mathematics, and 19th in reading.
In the 2022 PISA results, the Philippines ranked sixth from the bottom in reading and mathematics and third from the bottom in science, out of 81 participating countries.
In response to the 2022 performance, the advocacy group Philippine Business for Education warned that the country’s education system was in its “worst state”.

This year, the Philippines obtained a mean score of 373 in science, 371 in mathematics, and 367 in reading, representing increases of 17, 16, and 20 points, respectively, from the country’s 2022 Pisa results.

Data from OECD also showed that the Philippines is among the countries showing big changes between 2022 and 2025, with Georgia, Cambodia, Jordan, Montenegro, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Thailand, and Turkiye on top of the list.

The assessment, conducted by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), aims to evaluate the academic performance of more than 760,000 students aged 15 across partner countries every three years.
Highest score since joining

Education Secretary Sonny Angara on Tuesday announced the marked improvement in the Philippines’ performance, with Filipino students achieving their highest Pisa scores to date in reading, mathematics, and science.

Angara presented the results during the national launch at Caloocan City Science High School, highlighting gains across all three subject areas as he cited the Marcos administration’s continuing efforts to improve the country’s learning outcomes.
“This is a significant achievement for our learners and for the entire Philippine education system,” Angara said.

“But more than the numbers, we are seeing evidence that our learners are capable of making real and meaningful progress,” he added. “We should be proud of how far our learners and teachers have come, but we should be even more determined about how much farther we can go.”

Andreas Schleicher, OECD Director for Education and Skills, congratulated Filipino teachers and school leaders for the results, saying “what you have achieved in this latest round of OECD’s Pisa assessment is not just good news for the Philippines, it’s a story that deserves to be noticed far beyond your borders.”
The latest results show that the share of Filipino learners attaining Level 2 or higher, which is the baseline proficiency level under Pisa, has increased.
In science, the proportion rose from 23 percent to 32 percent; in mathematics, from 16 percent to 21 percent; and in reading, from 24 percent to 31 percent.
Bullying scores
However, Angara also noted that the Philippines recorded an increase in verbal and cyber bullying in schools compared to the 2022 Pisa results.
Based on the 2025 data, 33 percent of students claimed that other students made fun of them compared to the 22 percent reported in 2022.
Reports on the spread of rumors across students also increased from 15 percent to 19 percent in the latest assessment.
Reported experiences of physical bullying among Filipino students reflected only a one-percentage-point decrease from last year’s results, changing from 16 percent to 15 percent.
Meanwhile, reported threats between students remained at 19 percent in both the 2022 and 2025 Pisa results.
‘On the right track’
In a statement, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (Edcom 2) hailed the latest Pisa results and said the country’s educational reforms were “on the right track” and “gaining momentum.”

“This progress belongs to the entire country,” the commission said, noting that “over the past three years, teachers, parents, civil society organizations, volunteers, legislators, local government units, and communities have come together to confront the learning crisis and support every Filipino child.”
“This step forward demonstrates what we can achieve when the nation works together with urgency, purpose, and resolve,” it added. —With a report from Sheridan Delfino

articles.title: Remullas flying to France to seek help in finding Co
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla will also fly to France to follow up with the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) the Philippine government’s request for a…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla will also fly to France to follow up with the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) the Philippine government’s request for a red notice against resigned lawmaker and fugitive Zaldy Co.

Remulla disclosed this at a press briefing on Tuesday, after his brother, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla, said on Monday that he would travel to France to work with authorities there to find Co, who is believed to be seeking asylum in that country.

“We will again file a request for a red notice against Zaldy Co. Coincidentally, I am going to Lyon, France, to follow up [Co’s] red notice at the Interpol,” said the chief of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG).
Locate and arrest
An Interpol red notice is a request for law enforcement agencies worldwide to “locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action.”
“I will work with the Interpol. He (Ombudsman Remulla) will work with the diplomatic efforts [to get] Zaldy Co,” said the younger Remulla.
The Interpol’s headquarters are in Lyon, the city east of France that is widely acknowledged as the country’s culinary capital.
Co, who was charged in November last year in connection with a flood control project in Occidental Mindoro, was again the subject of an arrest warrant issued on Monday by the Sandiganbayan.

Apart from the resigned Ako Bicol party list lawmaker, the antigraft court also ordered the arrest of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez for plunder. The pair is accused of receiving around P7.44 billion in kickbacks from government projects between 2022 and 2025.

The amount, according to the information filed by the Office of the Ombudsman before the Sandiganbayan, allegedly came from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects that were funded under the General Appropriations Act for fiscal years 2022 to 2025.
Romualdez, who is confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for a “cardiovascular event,” has asked the court to allow him to remain at the hospital after his arrest.
In their motion for continued hospital confinement, his lawyers cited his “documented cardiac history,” diabetes and primary hypothyroidism, among other ailments. /cb

articles.title: Prosecutors opt to drop 15 witnesses, want to grill VP instead
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors on Tuesday dropped their remaining 15 witnesses on the alleged misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds and instead, manifested their intention to call…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors on Tuesday dropped their remaining 15 witnesses on the alleged misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds and instead, manifested their intention to call Vice President Sara Duterte to testify in her own impeachment trial, drawing an immediate objection from the defense.

Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said the prosecution had originally listed 27 witnesses for Article 1, which concerns the alleged misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds under the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd).
So far, 10 had been presented, while the parties had stipulated on the testimonies of two others. Three of the 15 remaining witnesses were scheduled to testify on Tuesday, Day 23 of the trial.
“In lieu of presenting 15 other witnesses, we will be presenting the Vice President herself as regards use, misuse, misappropriation of confidential funds,” Kapunan told the court.
She said the evidence already presented pointed to Duterte as the person accountable for the alleged irregularities.
VP ‘queen’ of confidential funds

“In the game chess, we have what we call pawns. There are bishops, there’s a castle, there are horses. And, the most important piece, more important than the king, and I speak this because not of my gender, but the queen is more important than the king, because the queen can move in many directions and we have seen that,” Kapunan said, using a chessboard analogy.

“We have seen that in the evidence presented, the pawns… the witnesses presented here. From the Landbank, we have been able to show that withdrawal, that there were confidential funds and these were withdrawn from two witnesses,” she added.
“All of these pawns and castles and horses and bishops point to only one person and that accountable person is the Vice President,” Kapunan declared.
But the prosecution did not seek a subpoena for Duterte yet, saying they intended to call her after presenting evidence on all four articles of impeachment.
Kapunan said Duterte’s testimony would be material to all four allegations—grave threats, misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds, unexplained wealth and bribery.
“Not at this time, your Honor,” Kapunan said when asked about a subpoena. “The testimony of the Vice President will be material to all four articles.”

The prosecution has completed its presentation on Article 4, which accuses Duterte of culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust over alleged threats against President Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former Speaker Martin Romualdez.
The articles on unexplained wealth and bribery remain to be presented.
Defense objection
The defense immediately objected to the prospect of Duterte being compelled to testify.
Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison said there was an “innate problem” with having Duterte testify in her own trial, citing the constitutional protection against testimonial compulsion.
Sison invoked Article III, Section 17 of the 1987 Constitution, which provides that no person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself or herself.
“This is a fundamental right,” she said, stressing that the protection emanates from the Constitution.Sison also said Duterte was already participating in the proceedings through her lawyers.
“It is clear that the respondent is here through her counsel. If the respondent is not interested in this trial, she would not have even sent her lawyers to defend her in this case,” she pointed out.
The defense reserved the right to file a formal comment if the prosecution later seeks a subpoena.
