articles.title: British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years
articles.summary: A 78-year-old British woman is facing deportation for failing to fill out a Brexit residence application on time.

blocks.text: A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brexit residence application.
Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, moved to Sweden 22 years ago with her husband, who passed away from cancer three years ago.
This came after they were informed by the Swedish authorities that they should have made a formal application to stay in the country after Brexit.
Thomas has since had numerous applications and appeals rejected, and Tuesday marks the latest deadline for her to leave voluntarily.
"This is absolute hell," she said from her home in Sweden.
"I can't sleep, I can't eat. You get up in the morning, you don't know what's going to happen."

The Swedish migration minister told the BBC that the government will "examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected" by some consequences of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement.
When the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.
During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under the withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.
Thomas said she and her husband were unaware that they needed to submit an application and she was only informed of the rule once she attempted to re-enter the country in 2023.
After years of appeals, the Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, told her last month that her voluntary departure deadline was 8 September.
Her lawyers are arguing against the deportation, but she is still waiting to hear from the government.
Thomas said the possibility of having to leave her son, grandchildren, friends and husband's grave has become too much to bear.
"I'm tired, I really am tired and I'm not young anymore," she said.
"Where is the empathy? I've lived here for more than 20 years - I've got friends, I've got family."

According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025, 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. This is almost a third of more than 7,500 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU Member States over this time period.
The Migrationsverket said it could not comment on Thomas's case without her consent and did not respond to a question about how many British nationals are at risk of deportation.
However, it told the Guardian last week that 458 British citizens had been deported or forcibly removed since Brexit.

Last month, a family told the BBC how their father, who has dementia and vascular parkinsonism and is living in full-time care in Sweden, was also threatened with removal after more than two decades in the country.

Swedish minister for migration, Johan Forssell, told the BBC that the current framework was implemented by a previous government and that it "will therefore look closely at the situation and examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected".
He did not address Thomas's case directly but said "the government believes the rules should be applied generously".
"The UK is a very important partner for Sweden, and we want British citizens who live and work in Sweden to be able to remain here," he said.
"We are currently in dialogue with the relevant Swedish authorities to get a clearer picture of what measures may be possible," he added.

A spokesperson from the the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: "We welcome the statement from the Swedish authorities that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so."

articles.title: Ratko Mladic’s funeral casts shadow over Bosnia and Herzegovina vote
articles.summary: Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade, attended by Serbian and Bosnian Serb leaders, has deepened regional tensions and could affect the upcoming election in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

image.caption: Mladic, who was dubbed the 'Butcher of Bosnia' for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, was buried with military honors in Serbia on MondayImage: Oliver Bunic/AFP

blocks.text: Belgrade has made a point of insisting that it did not organize a state funeral for former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladic, who was convicted of genocide in Srebrenica and crimes against humanity in 2017.

But when the body of a war criminal is flown home accompanied by the country's justice minister, when ceremonies unfold with military honors in state-controlled venues in the presence of senior political leaders and when clear condemnation of glorification of the deceased is absent, the message is unambiguous.
The impact of this message is being felt beyond Serbia's borders.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina — the state created by the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement, which comprises two entities linked by a weak central government — reactions were as deeply divided as the country itself.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: Two entities, two narratives
Republika Srpska, the Serb-majority entity covering about 49% of the country's territory, sent its officials to the funeral.

blocks.caption: Ratko Mladic was mourned by many in Republika Srpska, the majority Serb entity in Bosnia and HerzegovinaImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Public discourse there was dominated by narratives of "defending the people" and "the injustice of international courts."
"Without Ratko Mladic, there would be no Republika Srpska," was the refrain among thousands of mourners at the funeral in Belgrade.
Sarajevo, the seat of the central government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sees this approach as a continued policy of relativizing war crimes and a threat to stability.
Bosnia and Herzegovina cools diplomatic ties with Serbia
In the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the entity where Bosniaks and Croats form the majority, the response was very different and the tone sharp.
Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic described Serbia's official response as a conscious choice by Belgrade, not something imposed on it.

He announced measures to cool diplomatic ties with Serbia, withdrawing almost all staff from the country's embassy in Belgrade, leaving only the ambassador, explaining that he lacks the authority to close the embassy but can reduce its presence to a minimum. The move effectively froze day-to-day diplomatic communication on the ground.

blocks.caption: Bosnian Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic announced that he would be withdrawing almost all staff from the country's embassy in BelgradeImage: Denis Zuberi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: "We will pull out everyone we can; consular services will be relocated to Zagreb and Podgorica," he said.
Denis Becirovic, chair of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, called the funeral with military honors an "anti-civilizational act" and warned of far-reaching consequences for the entire region.
For representatives of Mladic's victims, any public glorification of the former general is a direct insult to the families of those killed.
Political point-scoring
Mladic's death and funeral are not just about the past.
At a time when both Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina are facing general elections — Bosnia on October 4 and Serbia likely just a few weeks later — emotions become a resource.
In both countries, parts of the electorate still see Mladic as a symbol of resistance, which means that every gesture in support of him scores political points with these voters.

As the general election in Bosnia and Herzegovina approaches, sharp condemnations from Sarajevo are seen as evidence that the central government is "defending the state" and "the dignity of victims." This, too, is being turned into political capital.

blocks.caption: Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina Denis Becirovic called Mladic's funeral with military honors an 'anti-civilizational act'Image: NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: In Republika Srpska, the presence of officials at the funeral and the narrative of "injustice" strengthen the position of those building their identity in opposition to international rulings.
Yet there are no "winners." The more political points anyone scores on this issue, the worse relations become and the further accession to the EU recedes into the distance — for both countries.

Tanja Topic, a political analyst from Banja Luka, is clear about who is responsible for these political narratives: "The main culprits are the political elites, because in 30 years we have not moved forward. There has been no critical confrontation with the dark side of history," she says. "This is a darkening of civilizational consciousness."
Topic went on to say that Mladic's funeral "is a welcome gift to the protagonists of ethno-nationalist policies" and noted that these people still hold power in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

"Such an institutional stance towards crimes provokes a reaction on the other side, and then everyone exploits the situation, trapping us in a vicious circle where each tries to extract political profit," Topic says.
A divided society and frozen relations

After Mladic's funeral, the Office of the High Representative (OHR) in Bosnia, which was created after the war to oversee the implementation of the US-brokered Dayton Peace Agreement, stressed that Bosnia's future cannot be built on glorifying those responsible for the worst crimes of the past.

blocks.caption: Mladic was convicted of genocide in Srebrenica, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the 1990s Bosnian War. Pictured here: headstones of victims of the July 1995 Srebrenica massacre Image: Elvis Barukcic/AFP

blocks.text: "Glorifying convicted war criminals, as well as denying genocide and other war crimes, creates divisions, inflicts additional pain on victims and their families, and undermines the reconciliation process," said the OHR.
Bosnia remains a deeply divided society that has not moved forward in the 31 years since the war ended.

The fact that the ideology that helped spark that war still lives on, means that Mladic's funeral did not close a chapter in the region's history, it tore open a new one, measuring the Balkans' willingness to step out of the shadow of the 1990s.
While politicians seek to score political points, citizens pay the price of frozen relations.

articles.title: BSW and AfD – a political love-hate relationship in Germany
articles.summary: The Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could help the Alternative for Germany (AfD) into power in Saxony-Anhalt. It is riddled with infighting

image.caption: AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund (top) could become head of government in Saxony-Anhalt with the support of the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW)Image: Karina Hessland-Wissel/Jan Huebner/IMAGO

blocks.text: Following the election in Saxony-Anhalt, there is no clear governing coalition because the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) with its 44% share of the vote has fallen just short of securing an absolute majority. That means the formation of a new government in one of Germany's 16 federal states is more difficult than ever. This is also partly due to the success that the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which was founded only in 2024, has managed to achieve. Wagenknecht, a trained economist, was a longtime member of the socialist Left Party, formerly a communist who over time has distanced herself further from her political roots. Her party does not conform to traditional labels. Many people can no longer relate much to labels like "left" or "right," she says.
From the very beginning, Wagenknecht also showed no reluctance to engage with the AfD. Her long-held credo has been that the party includes people who are treated unfairly if labeled as Nazis.
What next after far-right AfD win in regional election?

Now, Sahra Wagenknecht and her followers are working towards seeking common ground with the AfD and can even imagine helping the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund into the role of state premier by abstaining from the vote. Wagenknecht mentioned this scenario before the September 6 election.
Both AfD and BSW oppose 'uncontrolled migration'

A few days before the vote, Sahra Wagenknecht spoke on TV broadcaster ntv about overlapping policy preferences of BSW and AfD voters: "These are people who have similar concerns: They want controlled migration, they do not want this uncontrolled migration and they want above all that politics is again conducted in their interests, that their lives are the focus."

However, there is also a significant degree of agreement on issues other than German immigration policy: both parties call for an end to German arms deliveries to Ukraine, which has been attacked by Russia in violation of international law. Or they claim that freedom of speech no longer exists in Germany.

Whether the BSW will actually team up with the AfD remains completely open. AfD lead candidate Siegmund emphasized even before the election that he intended to govern only with an absolute majority of his own.

blocks.caption: Sahra Wagenknecht is no longer the chairwoman of the BSW party, but still its most prominent representativeImage: dts Nachrichtenagentur/IMAGO

blocks.text: When the BSW was founded in January 2024, it had a spectacular start: Formed as a splinter party from the socialist Left, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) was swiftly elected to the European Parliament and in the same year received double-digit results in three state parliament elections. In the eastern German states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party entered straight into government coalitions. That would also have been possible in Saxony, but coalition negotiations with the CDU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) failed.

The BSW favors a tough approach to refugees. It opposes any form of military support, whether for Ukraine or for Israel. The BSW advocates for an end to German weapons deliveries to Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia in breach of international law.

The party's leader, economist Sahra Wagenknecht, who grew up in communist East Germany, aligned her new political home beyond traditional classifications. She repeatedly states that many people can no longer relate to labels like "left" or "right" wing.
Wagenknecht has also had no reservations about contact with the AfD from the beginning. As early as 2023, she stated that some people within the party were being labeled Nazis unfairly.
Far left? Far right? What is Germany's BSW?
From rising star to struggling party

However, the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt has ruled out a classic coalition. Following elections in Brandenburg and Thuringia in 2024, the branches in those states went against the stated will of their founder and joined governments alongside established parties. The permanent conflict between the federal leadership of the party and its state branches led to the breakdown of the coalition with the Social Democrats in Brandenburg, starting in 2025.

In Thuringia, led by a coalition of the CDU, SPD and BSW, most of the BSW lawmakers declared that they were leaving the party two days before the election in Saxony-Anhalt. However, they wanted to remain a part of the CDU-led state government. "We have not been elected to tolerate flirts with right-wing radicals," is how Finance Minister Katja Wolf explained this decision, referring to the rapprochement with the AfD initiated by Wagenknecht.

The BSW's success in Saxony-Anhalt and accompanying key role in the formation of the government has given the party, at least for the moment, a largely unexpected significance. This is because during the Bundestag federal election of 2025 the BSW narrowly failed to reach the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament and, also due to its many internal conflicts, it seemed to have little credibility among the population.

Furthermore, its figurehead Sahra Wagenknecht has stepped back from the leadership of her party and is no longer running for its chairmanship. She continues to exert her influence in the background, though, and is a drawcard at BSW rallies, especially during election campaigns.
Boost for upcoming state elections?

Following their successful entry into Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which according to pre-election polls was by no means guaranteed, Wagenknecht responded confidently: "The BSW's comeback has begun," she told German news agency dpa. How sustainable this upswing is will be revealed on September 20, when parliamentary elections will be held in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state of Berlin.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing
articles.summary: In strongest condemnation ever by UK government, Ed Miliband announces sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements

blocks.text: Israeli “terrorists” are conducting ethnic cleansing in the West Bank with the tacit backing of the government, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has said as he announced sweeping sanctions, alongside France and Canada, on trade with Israeli settlements.

In the strongest condemnation ever issued by the UK government, Miliband said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, saying such acknowledgment was “the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”
Miliband said that the government would now enact:

items: An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.
A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements.
A ban on the advertising in the UK of illegal settlement properties.
Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.
A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.

blocks.text: Miliband said the action would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whose homes had been destroyed and from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.

The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.

Miliband said those who financed or facilitated illegal settlements would “face the full force of UK sanctions” and that he expected the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months.
He stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts.
Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.

“All too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians. I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”
He said the British government had previously described settlements as illegal but had not described the occupation itself as unlawful, and that would now change.

France and Canada were also announcing bans on settlement goods on Tuesday, joining the Netherlands, Ireland, Belgium, Spain and Norway, which have either banned goods or were in the process of doing so.
Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust.
“I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.

“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”

He said to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.

Miliband said he felt a “deep sense of shame about what has unfolded in Palestine under the eyes of the international community” and said there had been “the most unimaginable trauma and suffering in the last three years – death, destruction and dehumanisation on an appalling scale”.
The foreign secretary said the action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine; one that not only condemned but took action.
“Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”
Miliband said the actions of the Israeli government in the West Bank meant more settlements had been approved in the last four years than in the last 20 years combined.
He said he believed the majority of the British people would support the ban on trade with illegal settlements. “Settlements are illegal. They should not be promoted in our country,” he said.
The UK government knew there were also concerns about arm sales to Israel, he said. The UK had already suspended more than 30 arms licences used by the IDF in Gaza, but would now go further.

“We will now also refuse all licence applications for arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation, in effect a double lock against arms sales. This means the ban on such exports will now remain as long as the occupation persists.”
He said the UK would support “full, robust and fair judicial processes” to determine if Israel had committed genocide and said the government would not pre-judge that process.

“This has been the case for all of the genocides since the 1948 genocide convention: Rwanda, Srebrenica, Cambodia, and acts against the Yazidi people. This will remain our policy. It is right that this issue has been brought before the ICJ [international court of justice] and I want to make it clear that we support the court in coming to its determination.”

However, he said that the most recent reports by international bodies found there was “increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed and we support legal processes to determine this”.
The UK would use the UN general assembly next week to “shine the clearest and harshest spotlight on what is happening and what must change”.

The steps set out by Miliband fall short of the full demands made by Palestinian advocacy groups, but are a sign the UK is moving beyond traditional rhetorical support for a two-state solution towards active steps to forestall the expansion of illegal settlements in the West Bank.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to Donald Trump and key Gulf allies, such as Qatar, on Monday to brief them on the government’s plans in the region.

Both the US and Israel have threatened retaliation against Britain for the sanctions. The US ambassador to Israel, Mick Huckabee, said the US was considering what action to take, warning it may prohibit the UK from trade with several US states that have anti-BDS (boycott, divestment, sanctions) laws.
Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was “a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation” before the country’s elections in October.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Saar, said: “If Britain acts against Israel, Israel will act against Britain,” and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, called for the expulsion of the British ambassador.

articles.title: Argentina targets oil company operating in Falklands
articles.summary: The move comes days after President Javier Milei stepped up Argentina's claims of sovereignty over the Falklands.

blocks.text: The Argentine government has said that it would file criminal charges against oil company Navitas Petroleum for operating in seas off the Falkland Islands.
The move came just days after Argentine President Javier Milei said he would sanction oil companies drilling in the British overseas territory in the south-west Atlantic Ocean.
Sovereignty of the archipelago remains disputed between the UK and Argentina more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentine forces which had invaded the territory in 1982.
The simmering dispute heated up last week, when Milei said in a speech to the nation that the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the Falklands.
Milei has, in the past, been criticised by Argentine veterans of the 1982 conflict for being "too soft" on the Falklands, which Argentines call Las Malvinas.
In his speech on Thursday evening local time, Milei restated his government's position on the territory, saying "the Malvinas are Argentine, historically and legally... there's no debate about that."
The president described drilling for oil in the archipelago as a "clear and urgent danger" to Argentine sovereignty.
He also dismissed the result of a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands' residents voted in favour of the Falklands remaining a British oversees territory.
Milei argued that they were living on land which had been "usurped" by the British and therefore "have no legitimate right to self-determination".
The British government dismissed Milei's speech and stressed that its position on the Falklands was "unwavering".

Hopes that Milei's primetime speech may have been a blip and that he would return to his previous stance of strengthening diplomatic ties with the UK were crushed on Monday, however, when his office announced it would file criminal charges against Navitas Petroleum, several of its subsidiaries and their executives.
Navitas, which is listed in Tel Aviv, holds a 65% stake in Sea Lion, an offshore oil project set to start production in the North Falkland Basin in 2028.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
In Monday's statement, Milei alleged that drilling in the area would violate Argentine law banning resource exploitation without approval from the Argentine authorities.
"The state will continue to pursue actions deemed necessary to counter any act which breaches the sovereign rights of the Argentine Republic," the statement insisted.

Navitas has not yet responded to this latest statement but said last week that Milei's remarks were "not expected to have a material effect on the development activities of the Sea Lion Project, including the timetable for completion of the Project's development".
Rockhopper, which owns a partial stake in the Sea Lion project, has also not yet commented on Milei's statement.
Both companies have in the past stressed that Sea Lion holds valid licences from the Falkland Islands.

articles.title: Afghanistan's women: A national soccer team without a home
articles.summary: The Afghan women's national football team has finally been officially recognized by FIFA. Now the players want to make history both on and off the field.

image.caption: The Girl Power Summer Camps are a game changer for Afghanistan's women's teamImage: Irving Villegas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: On the football pitches of Bundesliga club Wolfsburg, the Afghanistan women's national team is training and doing exactly what is strictly forbidden in their home country: playing football.

In the first session of the day, the coaches' main focus is helping the players get to know each other better and have fun. That's because, as of April of this year, these young women are now officially allowed to play football as the Afghan national team.
FIFA, the world's football federation, has amended its regulations, allowing Afghan women to once again represent their country in official international matches and FIFA competitions.

"This was a huge victory for us, a wonderful moment, and one of the moments we're most proud of. Because once again, the women of our country have made history and brought about change," Khalida Popal told DW. The former captain and founder of the organization Girl Power has been a pioneer for women's football in her country.
Karimi: 'I'm incredibly proud'
Since the Taliban took power in 2021, the players and Popal have fought for the recognition that has now become a reality.
"I'm incredibly proud that we can now officially play as a national team," said midfielder Maryam Karimi.
For Karimi, who has been living in Portugal since fleeing Afghanistan, FIFA's decision is more than just a formality.
"I hope that one day we'll be able to play in Afghanistan again with this team."

blocks.caption: Almut Schult (fourth from the left) coaching the Afghanistan women's teamImage: Irving Villegas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Until then, however, Afghanistan remains a national team without a home.
"We'll probably be one of the first national teams in history that has no home and no country in which to play," said Popal. "We'll compete from exile and represent our country."
Today, the players are scattered across the world. Many have traveled from England, Italy, Portugal or Germany, but some have also found refuge in Australia.
"We come from different countries and can't play together regularly. But when I see the players, they're incredibly united. They keep going and push each other forward,” said Karimi.
Gaining More Visibility Through Football

The 39-year-old Popal wants to use her experience to help the players and advance their athletic development. She wants the national team to be known not only for what was taken from them, but also for what it achieves on the field.

"The first goal, of course, is to build a strong team that performs well on the field," said Popal. "Because the better we play, the better we can represent our country, and the more visible we'll become."

But that is precisely where the biggest challenge currently lies. In Afghanistan itself, a regular system for women's football cannot be established at this time. As long as the Taliban are in power, women are not allowed to play sports.

So there is nowhere for young talent to be nurtured; there is no funding and no support from the country the players represent. This is because the Afghan Football Federation — unlike FIFA — does not recognize the women's team. For the time being, therefore, the team's future must be built outside the country.

"We have no federation and no country where talent can develop," said Popal. That is why the team relies heavily on the Afghan diaspora. There, the team is looking for players who may never have played for a club in Afghanistan, but who could represent their parents' country in the future.
Popal: 'The Taliban are erasing women from society'

To organize football camps like these, the women rely on outside support. The summer 2026 camp was made possible by an invitation from Volkswagen and Wolfsburg, but Popal and her organization still have a lot of work ahead of them.

Giving players who have fled Afghanistan a place back in international football is one part of the challenge, but so is creating structures and a foundation on which Afghan women's football can be built.
"It will be a team that stands up to the Taliban. Because the Taliban are erasing women from society,” said Popal.
"We will play football to stand up for the women of our country. When the players take the field, they're also playing for those women in Afghanistan who aren't allowed to."

blocks.caption: Almuth Schult & Khalida Popal talking at Girl Power Summer CampImage: Irving Villegas/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Just like the former captain, the other young women on the team feel the same way. Midfielder Karimi wants to use football to draw more attention to her friends and all the women in her homeland.
"I can make my voice heard through the way I play football," Karimi said. "I can make my voice heard from the field."
Popal: "These girls are our future”

Despite a long battle for the human rights taken away from women by the Taliban, Popal keeps pushing because she wants to make sure that the women wearing the national team's jersey today are not the last generation to do so.

"I believe that Afghanistan won't stay this way forever. These dark days will pass. These girls will be the next coaches of the Afghan women's national team, the next directors of football academies, the next president, or the next ministers of our country," said Popal.
"And that is exactly why we are investing in these girls: because they are the future.”
This article was originally published in German.
